Warm surface water is pumped through an evaporator containing a working fluid in a closed Rankine-cycle system. The vaporized fluid drives a turbine/generator.

nodes.label: Octane
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Octane as: A flammable liquid hydrocarbon found in petroleum. Used as a standard to measure the anti-knock properties of motor fuel.

nodes.label: Octane rating
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Octane rating as: A number used to indicate gasoline's antiknock performance in motor vehicle engines. The two recognized laboratory engine test methods for determining the antiknock rating, i.e., octane rating, of gasolines are the Research method and the Motor method. To provide a single number as guidance to the consumer, the antiknock index (R + M)/2, which is the average of the Research and Motor octane numbers, was developed.

nodes.label: Off peak
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Off peak as: Period of relatively low system demand. These periods often occur in daily, weekly, and seasonal patterns; these off-peak periods differ for each individual electric utility.

nodes.label: Off-hours equipment reduction
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Off-hours equipment reduction as: A conservation feature where there is a change in the temperature setting or reduction in the use of heating, cooling, domestic hot water heating, lighting or any other equipment either manually or automatically.

nodes.label: Off-site produced energy for heat, power, and electricity generation
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Off-site produced energy for heat, power, and electricity generation as: This measure of energy consumption includes energy produced off-site and consumed on-site. It excludes primary energy produced and consumed on-site, energy used as raw material input, and electrical system energy losses.

nodes.label: Ohm
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Ohm as: A measure of the electrical resistance of a material equal to the resistance of a circuit in which the potential difference of 1 volt produces a current of 1 ampere.

nodes.label: Oil well
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Oil well as: A well completed for the production of crude oil from at least one oil zone or reservoir.

nodes.label: Oil well (casing head) gas
nodes.summary: The U.S. Energy Information Administration glossary defines Oil well (casing head) gas as: Associated and dissolved gas produced along with crude oil from oil completions.

nodes.label: First order logic
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B10) states: A logic is first order if it has exactly one type.

nodes.label: Propositional logic
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B05) states: A propositional logic is a logic in which the only objects are propositions , that is, objects which themselves have truth values.

nodes.label: Set theory
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 03E30) states: Set theory is special among mathematical theories, in two ways: It plays a central role in putting mathematics on a reliable axiomatic foundation , and it provides the basic language and apparatus in which most of mathematics is expressed.

nodes.label: Model theory
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 03C99) states: Model theory is a branch of mathematical logic which deals with the general problem of classifying mathematical structures.

nodes.label: Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (axiom entry, MSC 03E99) states: Ernst Zermelo and Abraham Fraenkel proposed the following axioms as a for what is now called Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory , or ZF.

nodes.label: Axiom of choice
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (axiom entry, MSC 03E30, 03E25) states: The Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms for set theory are often accepted as a basis for an axiomatic set theory .

nodes.label: Ordinal number
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03E10) states: An ordinal number is a well ordered set S such that, for every x ∈ S , x = { z ∈ S ∣ z < x } (where < is the ordering relation on S ).

nodes.label: Cardinal number
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03E10) states: A cardinal number is an ordinal number S with the property that S ≤ X for every ordinal number X which has the same cardinality as S .

nodes.label: Recursive function
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03D20) states: Intuitively, a recursive function is a positive integer valued function of one or more positive integer arguments which may be computed by a definite algorithm .

nodes.label: Gödel’s incompleteness theorems
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (theorem entry, MSC 03B10, 03F45) states: Gödel’s first and second incompleteness theorems are perhaps the most celebrated results in mathematical logic.

nodes.label: Modal logic
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 03B45) states: Introduction Modal logic is the logic of “ necessity ” and “possibility”.

nodes.label: Intuitionistic logic
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 03A05, 03B20, 03-01) states: Abstract The entry " intuitionistic logic " is a beginner’s introduction to the defining features of Brouwer’s (and his School) mathematical philosophy.

nodes.label: Lambda calculus
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B40) states: Lambda calculus (often referred to as λ -calculus) was invented in the 1930s by Alonzo Church, as a form of mathematical logic dealing primarly with functions and the application of functions to their arguments .

nodes.label: Cardinal arithmetic
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 03E10) states: Definitions Let κ and λ be cardinal numbers , and let A and B be disjoint sets such that | A | = κ and | B | = λ .

nodes.label: Logical connective
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B05) states: In propositional logic , the usual way of forming a well-formed formula out of existing ones is by attaching a designated symbol to the existing wffs.

nodes.label: Logical language
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B15, 03B10) states: In its most general form, a logical language is a set of rules for constructing formulas for some logic, which can then be assigned truth values based on the rules of that logic.

nodes.label: Quantifier
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B15, 03B10) states: Introduction A quantifier is a logical symbol which makes an assertion about the set of values which make one or more formulas true.

nodes.label: Arithmetical hierarchy
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B10) states: The arithmetical hierarchy is a hierarchy of either (depending on the context ) formulas or relations .

nodes.label: Biconditional
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03-00) states: 1 Biconditional A biconditional is a truth function that is true only in the case that both parameters are true or both are false.

nodes.label: Boolean-valued function
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 68Q01, 68P01, 06E30, 03G05, 03C55, 03B05, 68R01) states: A Boolean-valued function is a function of type f : X → 𝔹 , where X is an arbitrary set and where 𝔹 is a Boolean domain .

nodes.label: Derived Boolean operations
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 06E05, 03G05, 06B20, 03G10) states: Recall that a Boolean algebra is an algebraic system A consisting of five operations : 1.

nodes.label: Equivalence of forcing notions
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03E35, 03E40) states: Let P and Q be two forcing notions such that given any generic subset G of P there is a generic subset H of Q with 𝔐 ⁢ [ G ] = 𝔐 ⁢ [ H ] and vice-versa.

nodes.label: Equivalence relation
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 06-00, 03D20) states: An equivalence relation ∼ on a set S is a relation that is: Reflexive .

nodes.label: Equivalent machines
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03D05, 68Q45) states: Let M 1 = ( S 1 , Σ , Δ , σ 1 , λ 1 ) and M 2 = ( S 2 , Σ , Δ , σ 2 , λ 2 ) be two Mealy machines .

nodes.label: Filter basis
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03E99, 54A99) states: A filter subbasis for a set S is a collection of subsets of S which has the finite intersection property .

nodes.label: First order language
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03C07, 03B10) states: Let Σ be a signature . The first order language FO ⁡ ( Σ ) on Σ contains the following: 1.

nodes.label: Kripke semantics
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B48, 03B20, 03B45) states: A Kripke frame (or simply a frame) ℱ is a pair ( W , R ) where W is a non-empty set whose elements are called worlds or possible worlds , R is a binary relation on W called the accessibility relation .

nodes.label: Maximally consistent
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B05, 03B10, 03B99, 03B45) states: A set Δ of well-formed formulas (wff) is maximally consistent if Δ is consistent and any consistent superset of it is itself: Δ ⊆ Γ with Γ consistent implies Γ = Δ .

nodes.label: Propositional calculus
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03F03, 03C05, 03B22, 03B05) states: \PMlinkescapephrase adapted \PMlinkescapephrase Adapted \PMlinkescapephrase angle \PMlinkescapephrase Angle \PMlinkescapephrase calculus \PMlinkescapephrase Calculus \PMlinkescapephrase complete \PMlinkescapephrase Complete \PMlinkescapephrase component \PMlinkescapephrase Component \PMlinkescapephrase degree \PMlinkescapephrase Degree \PMlinkescapephrase formalism \PMlinkescapephrase Formalism \PMlinkescapephrase holder \PMlinkescapephrase Holder \PMlinkescapephrase holders \PMlinkescapephrase Holders \PMlinkescapephrase origin \PMlinkescapephrase Origin \PMlinkescapephrase plus \PMlinkescapephrase Plus \PMlinkescapephrase point \PMlinkescapephrase Point \PMlinkescapephrase points \PMlinkescapephrase Points \PMlinkescapephrase right \PMlinkescapephrase Right \PMlinkescapephrase utility \PMlinkescapephrase Utility A propositional calculus is a formal system whose expressions represent formal objects known as propositions and whose distinguished relations among expressions represent existing relations among propositions.

nodes.label: Substitutions in propositional logic
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B99) states: Uniform Substitution One area of mathematics where substitution plays a prominent role is mathematical logic.

nodes.label: Tautology
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B05, 03B10) states: A tautology is a statement (or form) which is true solely on account of its logical form rather than because of the meaning of the terms employed.

nodes.label: Truth function
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B05) states: A truth function is a function that returns one of two values, one of which is interpreted as “true,” and the other which is interpreted as “false”.

nodes.label: Truth table
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03-00, 34C29) states: A truth table is a tabular listing of all possible input value combinations for a logical function and their corresponding output values.

nodes.label: Truth-value semantics for classical propositional logic
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B05) states: In classical propositional logic , an interpretation of a well-formed formula (wff) p is an assignment of truth (=1) or falsity (=0) to p .

nodes.label: Axiom of foundation
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03C99) states: The axiom of foundation (also called the axiom of regularity ) is an axiom of ZF set theory prohibiting circular sets and sets with infinite levels of containment.

nodes.label: Extension of a function
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03E20) states: Let f : X → Y be a function and A and B be sets such that X ⊆ A and Y ⊆ B .

nodes.label: Natural number
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03E10, 74D99) states: Given the Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms of set theory , one can prove that there exists an inductive set X such that ∅ ∈ X .

nodes.label: Ordered pair
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03-00, 70A05, 70G99) states: For any sets a and b , the ordered pair ( a , b ) is the set { { a } , { a , b } } .

nodes.label: Restriction of a function
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03E20) states: Definition Let f : X → Y be a function from a set X to a set Y .

nodes.label: Satisfaction relation
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03C07) states: Alfred Tarski was the first mathematician to give a formal definition of what it means for a formula to be “true” in a structure .

nodes.label: Structure homomorphism
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03C07) states: Let Σ be a fixed signature , and 𝔄 and 𝔅 be two structures for Σ .

nodes.label: Subfunction
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 08A55, 03E20) states: Definition . Let f : A → B and g : C → D be partial functions .

nodes.label: Substructure
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03C07) states: Let Σ be a fixed signature , and 𝔄 and 𝔅 structures for Σ .

nodes.label: Algebraic system
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 08A05, 03E99, 08A62) states: An algebraic system , loosely speaking, is a set, together with some operations on the set.

nodes.label: Concept lattice
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 68Q55, 68P99, 08A70, 06B23, 03B70, 06A15) states: Let G and M be sets whose elements we call objects and attributes respectively.

nodes.label: Elementary embedding
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03C99) states: Let τ be a signature and 𝒜 and ℬ be two structures for τ such that f : 𝒜 → ℬ is an embedding .

nodes.label: Formal grammar
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 91F20, 68Q42, 68Q45, 03D05) states: Introduction A grammar , loosely speaking, is a set of rules that can be applied to words to generate sentences in a language .

nodes.label: From Hilbert’s tenth problem to Gödel’s trichotomy
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 03A05, 03-01) states: From Hilbert’s tenth problem to Gödel’s trichotomy Contents: 1 Hilbert on the pursuit of knowledge 2 The two sources of mathematical knowledge 3 Hilbert’s epistemological optimism 4 Stricto sensu and conditional mathematics 5 The cumulative hierarchy 6 Diophantine equivalent of number theoretical statements 7 The incompleteness and consistency propositions 8 Sketch of a Gedankenexperiment 9 Gödel’s trichotomy 1 Hilbert on the pursuit of knowledge In the Summer of 1900 the Second International Congress of Mathematicians took place in Paris and Hilbert’s paper to the Congress has the form of a statement of the strategical goals to be pursued by the discipline.

nodes.label: Imaginaries
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03C95, 03C68) states: Given an algebraic structure S to investigate, mathematicians consider substructures , restrictions of the structure , quotient structures and the like.

nodes.label: O-minimality
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03C64, 14P10) states: Let M be an ordered structure . An interval in M is any subset of M that can be expressed in one of the following forms: • { x : a < x < b } for some a , b from M • { x : x > a } for some a from M • { x : x < a } for some a from M Then we define M to be o-minimal iff every definable subset of M is a finite union of intervals and points.

nodes.label: Quantifier free
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03C10, 03C07, 03B10) states: Let L be a first order language . A formula ψ is quantifier free iff it contains no quantifiers .

nodes.label: Signature of a permutation
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03-00, 05A05, 20B99) states: Let X be a finite set , and let G be the group of permutations of X (see permutation group ).

nodes.label: Axiom
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B99, 03A05) states: In a nutshell, the logico-deductive method is a system of inference where conclusions (new knowledge) follow from premises (old knowledge) through the application of sound arguments ( syllogisms , rules of inference ).

nodes.label: Axiom of infinity
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (axiom entry, MSC 03E30) states: There exists an infinite set . The Axiom of Infinity is an axiom of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory .

nodes.label: Classes of ordinals and enumerating functions
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03F15, 03E10) states: A class of ordinals is just a subclass of the class ( http://planetmath.org/Class ) 𝐎𝐧 of all ordinals.

nodes.label: Continuum hypothesis
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (axiom entry, MSC 03E50) states: The continuum hypothesis that there is no cardinal number κ such that ℵ 0 < κ < 2 ℵ 0 .

nodes.label: Empty set
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03-00, 65H05, 65H10) states: An empty set is a set ∅ that contains no elements .

nodes.label: Generalized Cartesian product
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03E20) states: Given any family of sets { A j } j ∈ J indexed by an index set J , the generalized Cartesian product ∏ j ∈ J A j is the set of all functions f : J → ⋃ j ∈ J A j such that f ⁢ ( j ) ∈ A j for all j ∈ J .

nodes.label: Hausdorff’s maximum principle
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (theorem entry, MSC 03E25) states: Theorem Let X be a partially ordered set . Then there exists a maximal totally ordered subset of X .

nodes.label: Hilbert system
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03F03, 03B99, 03B22) states: A Hilbert system is a style (formulation) of deductive system that emphasizes the role played by the axioms in the system.

nodes.label: Injective function
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03E20, 03E99) states: We say that a function f : A → B is injective or one-to-one if f ⁢ ( x ) = f ⁢ ( y ) implies x = y , or equivalently, whenever x ≠ y , then f ⁢ ( x ) ≠ f ⁢ ( y ) .

nodes.label: Surjective
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03-00) states: A function f : X → Y is called surjective or onto if, for every y ∈ Y , there is an x ∈ X such that f ⁢ ( x ) = y .

nodes.label: Uncountable
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03E10) states: Definition A set is uncountable if it is not countable .

nodes.label: Ordering relation
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03-00, 81-00, 18-00, 17B37, 18D10, 18D35, 16W30) states: Let S be a set. An ordering relation is a relation ≤ on S such that, for every a , b , c ∈ S : • Either a ≤ b , or b ≤ a , • If a ≤ b and b ≤ c , then a ≤ c , • If a ≤ b and b ≤ a , then a = b .

nodes.label: Ordinal arithmetic
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 03E10) states: Ordinal arithmetic is the extension of normal arithmetic to the transfinite ordinal numbers.

nodes.label: Cardinality
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03E10) states: Cardinality Cardinality is a notion of the size of a set which does not rely on numbers.

nodes.label: Automaton
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03D05, 68Q45) states: An automaton is a semiautomaton with two types of special states: starting states, and final states.

nodes.label: Combinatory logic
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B40) states: Combinatory logic was invented by Moses Schönfinkel in the early 1920s, and was mostly developed by Haskell Curry.

nodes.label: Recursively enumerable
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03D25) states: For a language L , TFAE: • There exists a Turing machine f such that ∀ x .

nodes.label: Alternative characterizations of recursive functions
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 03D20) states: The class of recursive functions may be characterized by considerably weaker conditions than those given in the entry “recursive function ( http://planetmath.org/RecursiveFunction )” of this encyclopaedia.

nodes.label: Primitive recursive function
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03D20) states: To define what a primitive recursive function is, the following notations are used: ℱ = ⋃ { F k ∣ k ∈ ℕ } , where for each k ∈ ℕ ⁢ , ⁢ F k = { f ∣ f : ℕ k → ℕ } .

nodes.label: Turing computable
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03D10, 68Q05) states: A function is Turing computable if the function’s value can be computed with a Turing machine .

nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 03B10, 03A05, 03-01) states: Contents: 1 Overview 2 Arithmetic 3 From the number sequence to formal arithmetic 4 The formal theory Z 5 A model for Z 6 Gödel numbers 7 Expressing relations and representing functions in Z 8 Omega-consistency and metamathematical predicates 9 How to build Gödel’s undecidable statement 10 Gödel’s first theorem 11 The interpretation of the undecidable formula 12 Gödel’s second theorem 13 The interpretation of the second theorem 14 The concept of truth A Q & A 1 Overview In the literature on the foundations of mathematics the term ” formalism ” occurs with three different configurations .

nodes.label: Contradiction
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03F07, 03B05) states: A contradiction occurs when the statements p and ¬ ⁢ p are shown to be true simultaneously.

nodes.label: Contradictory statement
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B05) states: A contradictory statement is a statement (or form) which is false due to its logical form rather than because of the meaning of the terms employed.

nodes.label: Necessary and sufficient
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B05, 03F07) states: The statement “ p is necessary for q ” “ q implies ( http://planetmath.org/ Implication ) p ”.

nodes.label: Russell’s theory of types
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B15) states: After the discovery of the paradoxes of set theory (notably Russell’s paradox ), it become apparent that naive set theory must be replaced by something in which the paradoxes can’t arise.

nodes.label: Axiom system for first order logic
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B10) states: Let FO ( Σ ) be a first order language over signature Σ .

nodes.label: Axiom system for propositional logic
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B05) states: The language of (classical) propositional logic PL c consists of a set of propositional letters or variables , the symbol ⟂ (for falsity), together with two symbols for logical connectives ¬ and → .

nodes.label: Deduction
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03F03, 03B99, 03B22) states: Deductions are formalizations of proofs. Informally, they can be viewed as arriving at a conclusion from a set of assumptions, via applications of some prescribed rules in a finite number of steps.

nodes.label: Formal system
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 03B99) states: In mathematical logic, a formal system is a “set-up” to study the syntactic structures of statements that we see in everyday mathematics.

nodes.label: Inference rule
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B35, 03B22, 03B05) states: In logic, an inference rule is a rule whereby one may correctly draw a conclusion from one or more premises .

nodes.label: Logical axiom
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 03B22, 03B05) states: In a logical system , a logical axiom (sometimes called an axiom for short) is a logically valid (well-formed) formula used in a deductive system (particularly an axiom system ) to deduce other logically valid formulas.

nodes.label: Logically equivalent
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B05) states: Two formulas A and B are said to be logically equivalent (typically shortened to equivalent ) when A is true if and only if B is true (that is, A implies B and B implies A ): ⊧ A ↔ B .

nodes.label: Modus ponens
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B22, 03B05, 03B35) states: Modus ponens is a rule of inference that is commonly found in many logics where the binary logical connective → (sometimes written ⇒ or ⊃ ) called logical implication are defined.

nodes.label: Normal modal logic
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03B45) states: The study of modal logic is based on the concept of a logic , which is a set Λ of wff’s satisfying the following: • contains all tautologies , and • is closed under modus ponens .

nodes.label: Power set
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03E99, 03E10, 37-01) states: Definition If X is a set, then the power set of X , denoted by 𝒫 ⁢ ( X ) , is the set whose elements are the subsets of X .

nodes.label: Quantum logic
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03G12) states: Introduction In classical physics, results regarding experiments performed on physical propositions obey classical propositional logic .

nodes.label: Analytics and formal logics in meta-mathematics
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 53B21, 03G30, 03G20, 03B22, 01A60, 18-00, 03G30, 46M15, 03B22, 03B50, 03B15) states: This is a topic on meta-theories , metalogic and metamathematics founded in formal logic .

nodes.label: Chu space
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03G99) states: A Chu space over a set Σ is a triple ( 𝒜 , r , 𝒳 ) with r : 𝒜 × 𝒳 → Σ .

nodes.label: Elementary recursive function
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03D20) states: Informally, elementary recursive functions are functions that can be obtained from functions encountered in elementary schools: addition , multiplication , subtraction , and division , using basic operations such as substitutions and finite summation and product .

nodes.label: Free and bound variables
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 03C07, 03B10) states: In the entry first-order language ( http://planetmath.org/TermsAndFormulas ), I have mentioned the use of variables without mentioning what variables really are.

nodes.summary: PlanetMath (theorem entry, MSC 26A06) states: The product rule states that if f : ℝ → ℝ and g : ℝ → ℝ are functions in one variable both differentiable at a point x 0 , then the derivative of the product of the two functions, denoted f ⋅ g , at x 0 is given by d d ⁢ x ⁢ ( f ⋅ g ) ⁢ ( x 0 ) = f ⁢ ( x 0 ) ⁢ g ′ ⁢ ( x 0 ) + f ′ ⁢ ( x 0 ) ⁢ g ⁢ ( x 0 ) .

nodes.label: Quotient rule
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (theorem entry, MSC 26A06) states: The quotient rule says that the derivative of the quotient f / g of two differentiable functions f and g exists at all values of x as long as g ⁢ ( x ) ≠ 0 and is given by the formula d d ⁢ x ⁢ [ f ⁢ ( x ) g ⁢ ( x ) ] = g ⁢ ( x ) ⁢ f ′ ⁢ ( x ) - f ⁢ ( x ) ⁢ g ′ ⁢ ( x ) [ g ⁢ ( x ) ] 2 The Quotient Rule and the other differentiation formulas allow us to compute the derivative of any rational function .

nodes.label: Related rates
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 53A45, 53A17, 26A24) states: The notion of a derivative has numerous interpretations and applications.

nodes.label: Similar matrix
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 15A03) states: Definition A square matrix A is similar (or conjugate ) to a square matrix B if there exists a nonsingular square matrix S such that A = S - 1 ⁢ B ⁢ S .

nodes.label: Tangent line
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 26B05, 26A24) states: If the curve y = f ⁢ ( x ) of x ⁢ y -plane is sufficiently smooth in its point ( x 0 , y 0 ) and in a neighborhood of this, the curve may have a tangent line (or simply ) in ( x 0 , y 0 ) .

nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 46E40) states: Vector fields in ℝ n Definition . A vector field v on some open set U ⊂ R n is a function which associates a vector v ⁢ ( x ) to each point x of U .

nodes.label: Incidence geometry
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 05B35, 06C10, 51A05) states: Incidence geometry is essentially geometry based on the first postulate in Euclid’s The Elements .

nodes.label: Incidence structure

nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 05C75) states: A pseudograph is a graph that allows both parallel edges and loops.

nodes.label: Connected space
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 54D05) states: A topological space X is said to be connected if there is no pair of nonempty subsets U , V such that both U and V are open in X , U ∩ V = ∅ and U ∪ V = X .

nodes.label: Differentiable function
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 26A24, 57R35) states: Let f : V → W be a function , where V and W are Banach spaces .

nodes.label: Homeomorphism
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 54C05) states: A homeomorphism f of topological spaces is a continuous , bijective map such that f - 1 is also continuous.

nodes.label: Metric equivalence
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 54E35) states: Let X be a set equipped with two metrics ρ and σ . We say that ρ is equivalent to σ (on X ) if the identity map on X , is a homeomorphism between the metric topology on X induced by ρ and the metric topology on X induced by σ .

nodes.label: Metrizable
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 54-00, 55-00, 22-00) states: A topological space ( X , 𝒯 ) is said to be metrizable if there is a metric d : X → [ 0 , ∞ ) such that the topology induced by d is 𝒯 .

nodes.label: Paracompact topological space
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 54-00, 55-00) states: A topological space X is said to be paracompact if every open cover of X has a locally finite open refinement.

nodes.label: Second countable
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 54D70) states: A topological space is said to be second if it has a countable basis ( http://planetmath.org/BasisTopologicalSpace ).

nodes.label: Submanifold
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 32V40, 53C40, 53B25, 57N99) states: There are several conflicting definitions of what a submanifold is, depending on which author you are reading.

nodes.label: Total differential
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 53A04, 26B05, 01A45) states: There is the generalisation of the theorem in the parent entry ( http:// planetmath .org/ Differential ) concerning the real functions of several variables; here we formulate it for three variables: Theorem.

nodes.label: Change of basis
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 15A04) states: Let V be a vector space . Given a basis A for V , each vector v ∈ V can be uniquely expressed in terms of the base elements v i ∈ A as follows: v = ∑ v i ∈ A r i ⁢ v i where the sum is taken over a finite number of elements in A .

nodes.label: Determinant

nodes.label: Dimension (vector space)

nodes.label: List vector
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 15A03, 15A90) states: Let 𝕂 be a field and n a positive natural number. We define 𝕂 n to be the set of all mappings from the index list ( 1 , 2 , … , n ) to 𝕂 .

nodes.label: Projective basis
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 05B35, 06C10, 51A05) states: In the parent entry, we see how one may define dimension of a projective space inductively, from its subspaces starting with a point, then a line, and working its way up.

nodes.label: Sesquilinear forms over general fields
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 47A07, 15A63, 11E39, 51A05) states: Let V be a vector space over a field k . k may be of any characteristic .

nodes.label: Transpose
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 15A57) states: The transpose of a matrix A is the matrix formed by “flipping” A about the diagonal line from the upper left corner.

nodes.label: Absolute value
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 13-00, 11A15) states: Let R be an ordered ring and let a ∈ R . The absolute value of a is defined to be the function | | : R → R given by | a | := { a if ⁢ a ≥ 0 , - a otherwise.

nodes.label: Absolute value in a vector lattice
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 46A40, 06F20) states: Let V be a vector lattice over ℝ , and V + be its positive cone .

nodes.label: Ascending order
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 06A99) states: A sequence or arbitrary ordered set or one-dimensional array of numbers, a , is said to be in ascending order if each a i ≤ a i + 1 .

nodes.label: Coefficients of a polynomial
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 08A40) states: If p ⁢ ( x ) = ∑ i = 0 n a i ⁢ x i is a polynomial ( http://planetmath.org/BasicPolynomial ), then its coefficients are { a i } i = 0 n .

nodes.label: Complex number
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 12D99, 30-00, 32-00, 46L05, 18B40, 46M20, 17B37, 22A22, 81R50, 22D25) states: The ring of complex numbers ℂ is defined to be the quotient ring of the polynomial ring ℝ ⁢ [ X ] in one variable over the reals by the principal ideal ( X 2 + 1 ) .

nodes.label: Descending order
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 06A99) states: A sequence or arbitrary ordered set or one-dimensional array of numbers, a , is said to be in descending order if each a i ≥ a i + 1 .

nodes.label: Fraction
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 11-01) states: A fraction is a rational number expressed in the form n d or n / d , where n is designated the numerator and d the denominator .

nodes.label: Modulus of complex number
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 32-00, 30-00, 12D99) states: Definition Let z be a complex number , and let z ¯ be the complex conjugate of z .

nodes.label: Monomial
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 12-00) states: A monomial is a product of non-negative powers of variables .

nodes.label: Polynomial ring

nodes.label: Polynomials in algebraic systems
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 08A40) states: Polynomials in an Algebraic System Let ( A , O ) be an algebraic system .

nodes.label: Radical of an ideal
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 14A05, 16N40, 13-00) states: Let R be a commutative ring . For any ideal I of R , the radical of I , written I or Rad ⁡ ( I ) , is the set { a ∈ R ⁢ ∣ a n ∈ I ⁢ for some integer ⁢ n > ⁢ 0 } The radical of an ideal I is always an ideal of R .

nodes.label: Radical of an integer
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 13A10, 81-00, 18-00) states: Given a natural number n , let n = p 1 α 1 ⁢ ⋯ ⁢ p k α k be its unique factorization as a product of distinct prime powers.

nodes.label: Real number
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 54C30, 26-00, 12D99) states: 1 Definition There are several equivalent definitions of real number , all in common use.

nodes.label: Differential operator
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 53-00, 35-00, 47E05, 47F05) states: Roughly speaking, a differential operator is a mapping , typically understood to be linear, that transforms a function into another function by means of partial derivatives and multiplication by other functions.

nodes.label: Wave equation
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 35L05) states: The wave equation is a partial differential equation which describes certain kinds of waves.

nodes.label: Zero of a function
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 26E99) states: \PMlinkescapephrase closed set Suppose X is a set and f a complex ( http://planetmath.org/Complex )-valued function f : X → ℂ .

nodes.label: Borel space
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 60A10, 28C15, 28A12, 54H05, 28A05) states: Definition 0.1 . A Borel space ( X ; ℬ ⁢ ( X ) ) is defined as a set X , together with a Borel σ - algebra ( http://planetmath.org/SigmaAlgebra ) ℬ ⁢ ( X ) of subsets of X , called Borel sets .

nodes.label: Distribution function
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 60E05) states: [this entry is currently being revised, so hold off on corrections until this line is removed] Let F : ℝ → ℝ .

nodes.label: Extended real numbers
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 28-00, 12D99) states: The extended real numbers are the real numbers together with + ∞ (or simply ∞ ) and - ∞ .

nodes.label: Measurable space

nodes.label: Commutative language
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 68Q70) states: Let Σ be an alphabet and u a word over Σ . Write u as a product of symbols in Σ : u = a 1 ⁢ ⋯ ⁢ a n where a i ∈ Σ .

nodes.label: Homomorphism of languages
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 68Q45) states: Let Σ 1 and Σ 2 be two alphabets . A function h : Σ 1 * → Σ 2 * is called a homomorphism if it is a semigroup homomorphism from semigroups Σ 1 * to Σ 2 * .

nodes.label: McAlister covering theorem
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (theorem entry, MSC 20M18) states: A subset X in an inverse semigroup S is called unitary if for any elements x ∈ X and s ∈ S , x ⁢ s ∈ X or s ⁢ x ∈ X implies s ∈ X .

nodes.label: Monoid
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 20M99, 34-01) states: A monoid is a semigroup G which contains an identity element ; that is, there exists an element e ∈ G such that e ⋅ a = a ⋅ e = a for all a ∈ G .

nodes.label: Quotient group
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 20-00) states: Before defining quotient groups , some preliminary definitions must be introduced and a few established.

nodes.label: Semigroup
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 20M99) states: A semigroup G is a set together with a binary operation ⋅ : G × G ⟶ G which satisfies the associative property: ( a ⋅ b ) ⋅ c = a ⋅ ( b ⋅ c ) for all a , b , c ∈ G .

nodes.label: Biops
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 08A99) states: Let S be a set and n ∈ 𝐍 . Set 𝐍 n := { i ∈ 𝐍 | i < n } . If there exists a map ⋅ : 𝐍 n → ( S 2 → S ) : i ↦ ⋅ i where ⋅ i : S 2 → S : ( a , b ) ↦ a ⋅ i b is a binary operation , then I shall say that ( S , ⋅ ) is an n -biops .

nodes.label: Division
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 00A05, 12E99) states: Division is the operation which assigns to every two numbers (or more generally, elements of a field) a and b their quotient or ratio, provided that the latter, b , is distinct from zero.

nodes.label: Expression
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 00-01) states: An expression is a symbol or of symbols used to denote a quantity or value.

nodes.label: Characteristic subgroup
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 20A05) states: If ( G , * ) is a group, then H is a characteristic subgroup of G (written H ⁢ char ⁡ G ) if every automorphism of G maps H to itself.

nodes.label: Section of a group
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 20F99) states: A section of a group G is a quotient ( http://planetmath.org/QuotientGroup ) of a subgroup of G .

nodes.label: Singleton
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 00A05) states: A singleton is a set containing a single element.

nodes.label: Variable
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 00A05) states: The word variable as used in mathematics (and in other scientific fields that use mathematics) is somewhat vague and may have different meanings depending on the context .

nodes.label: Group representation
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 20C99) states: Let G be a group, and let V be a vector space . A representation of G in V is a group homomorphism ρ : G → GL ⁡ ( V ) from G to the general linear group GL ⁡ ( V ) of invertible linear transformations of V .

nodes.label: Closure of a subset under relations
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 08A02) states: Let A be a set and R be an n -ary relation on A , n ≥ 1 . A subset B of A is said to be closed under R , or R -closed , if, whenever b 1 , … , b n - 1 ∈ B , and ( b 1 , … , b n - 1 , b n ) ∈ R , then b n ∈ B .

nodes.label: Coset
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 20A05) states: Let H be a subgroup of a group G , and let a ∈ G . The left coset of a with respect to H in G is defined to be the set a ⁢ H := { a ⁢ h ∣ h ∈ H } .

nodes.label: Left identity and right identity

nodes.label: Concepts in abstract algebra
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 55-00, 18-00, 16-00, 13-00, 20-00, 15-00) states: The aim of this entry is to present a list of the key operators used in abstract algebra .

nodes.label: Euclidean space
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 15A03, 51M05) states: 1 Definition Euclidean n -space is a metric space ( E , d ) with the property that the group of isometries is transitive and is isomorphic to an n -dimensional Euclidean vector space .

nodes.label: Fractional ideal of commutative ring

nodes.label: Higher-order function

nodes.label: Cross product

nodes.label: Dimension
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 00-01, 15A03, 54F45) states: The word dimension in mathematics has many definitions, but all of them are trying to quantify our intuition that, for example, a sheet of paper has somehow one less dimension than a stack of papers.

nodes.label: Dot product

nodes.label: Separation axioms

nodes.label: T3 space
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 54D10) states: A regular space is a topological space in which points and closed sets can be separated by open sets ; in other words, given a closed set A and a point x ∉ A , there are disjoint open sets U and V such that x ∈ U and A ⊆ V .

nodes.label: Tychonoff space

nodes.label: Von Neumann regular

nodes.label: Maximal subgroup
nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 20E28) states: Let G be a group. A subgroup H of G is said to be a maximal subgroup of G if H ≠ G and there is no subgroup K of G such that H < K < G .

nodes.label: Negative number

nodes.label: Closure map

nodes.label: biological phase
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines biological phase as: A distinct period or stage in a biological process or cycle.

nodes.label: pigmentation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines pigmentation as: The accumulation of pigment in an organism, tissue or cell, either by increased deposition or by increased number of cells.

nodes.label: growth
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines growth as: The increase in size or mass of an entire organism, a part of an organism or a cell.

nodes.label: viral process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral process as: A multi-organism process in which a virus is a participant. The other participant is the host. Includes infection of a host cell, replication of the viral genome, and assembly of progeny virus particles. In some cases the viral genetic material may integrate into the host genome and only subsequently, under particular circumstances, 'complete' its life cycle.

nodes.label: reproductive process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines reproductive process as: A biological process that directly contributes to the process of producing new individuals by one or two organisms. The new individuals inherit some proportion of their genetic material from the parent or parents.

nodes.label: immune system process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines immune system process as: Any process involved in the development or functioning of the immune system, an organismal system for calibrated responses to potential internal or invasive threats.

nodes.label: cellular process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cellular process as: Any process that is carried out at the cellular level, but not necessarily restricted to a single cell. For example, cell communication occurs among more than one cell, but occurs at the cellular level.

nodes.label: locomotion
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines locomotion as: Self-propelled movement of a cell or organism from one location to another.

nodes.label: rhythmic process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines rhythmic process as: Any process pertinent to the generation and maintenance of rhythms in the physiology of an organism.

nodes.label: biological regulation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines biological regulation as: Any process that modulates a measurable attribute of any biological process, quality or function.

nodes.label: biological process involved in intraspecies interaction between organisms
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines biological process involved in intraspecies interaction between organisms as: Any process in which an organism has an effect on an organism of the same species.

nodes.label: developmental process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines developmental process as: A biological process whose specific outcome is the progression of an integrated living unit: an anatomical structure (which may be a subcellular structure, cell, tissue, or organ), or organism over time from an initial condition to a later condition.

nodes.label: multicellular organismal process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines multicellular organismal process as: Any biological process, occurring at the level of a multicellular organism, pertinent to its function.

nodes.label: biological process involved in interspecies interaction between organisms
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines biological process involved in interspecies interaction between organisms as: Any process evolved to enable an interaction with an organism of a different species.

nodes.label: localization
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines localization as: Any process in which a cell, a substance, or a cellular entity, such as a protein complex or organelle, is transported, tethered to or otherwise maintained in a specific location. In the case of substances, localization may also be achieved via selective degradation.

nodes.label: homeostatic process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines homeostatic process as: Any biological process involved in the maintenance of an internal steady state. Homeostasis allows cells and organisms to maintain stable internal conditions despite varying external conditions.

nodes.label: detoxification
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines detoxification as: Any process that reduces or removes the toxicity of a toxic substance. These may include transport of the toxic substance away from sensitive areas and to compartments or complexes whose purpose is sequestration of the toxic substance.

nodes.label: virion component
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virion component as: Any constituent part of a virion, a complete fully infectious extracellular virus particle.

nodes.label: cellular anatomical structure
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cellular anatomical structure as: A part of a cellular organism that is either an immaterial entity or a material entity with granularity above the level of a protein complex but below that of an anatomical system. Or, a substance produced by a cellular organism with granularity above the level of a protein complex.

nodes.label: protein-containing complex
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines protein-containing complex as: A stable assembly of two or more macromolecules, i.e. proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates or lipids, in which at least one component is a protein and the constituent parts function together.

nodes.label: single-celled organism vegetative growth phase
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines single-celled organism vegetative growth phase as: A phase of population growth during which single celled organisms reproduce by budding, fission, or other asexual methods.

nodes.label: hair cycle phase
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines hair cycle phase as: The cyclical periods of growth (anagen), regression (catagen), quiescence (telogen), and shedding (exogen) in the life of a hair; one of the collection or mass of filaments growing from the skin of an animal, and forming a covering for a part of the head or for any part or the whole of the body.

nodes.label: anestrus phase
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines anestrus phase as: A biological phase of reproductive dormancy characterized by the temporary cessation of reproductive cyclicity, marked by the absence of ovarian follicular development, estrous behavior, and ovulation. This phase represents a period of sexual quiescence between estrous cycles or breeding seasons.

nodes.label: estrous cycle phase
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines estrous cycle phase as: The progression of physiological phases, occurring in the endometrium during the estrous cycle that recur at regular intervals during the reproductive years. The estrous cycle is an ovulation cycle where the endometrium is resorbed if pregnancy does not occur.

nodes.label: reproductive senescence
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines reproductive senescence as: A life cycle stage during which the reproductive capacity and fitness of an organism declines.

nodes.label: menstrual cycle phase
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines menstrual cycle phase as: The progression of physiological phases, occurring in the endometrium during the menstrual cycle that recur at regular intervals during the reproductive years. The menstrual cycle is an ovulation cycle where the endometrium is shed if pregnancy does not occur.

nodes.label: cell cycle phase
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell cycle phase as: One of the distinct periods or stages into which the cell cycle is divided. Each phase is characterized by the occurrence of specific biochemical and morphological events.

nodes.label: developmental pigmentation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines developmental pigmentation as: The developmental process that results in the deposition of coloring matter in an organism, tissue or cell.

nodes.label: ocellus pigmentation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ocellus pigmentation as: The deposition or aggregation of coloring matter in an ocellus, a minute simple eye found in many invertebrates.

nodes.label: pigment accumulation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines pigment accumulation as: The aggregation of coloring matter in a particular location in an organism, tissue or cell, occurring in response to some external stimulus.

nodes.label: cellular pigmentation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cellular pigmentation as: The deposition or aggregation of coloring matter in a cell.

nodes.label: primary growth
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines primary growth as: Growth of a plant structure from the time of its initiation by an apical meristem until its expansion is completed.

nodes.label: developmental growth
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines developmental growth as: The increase in size or mass of an entire organism, a part of an organism or a cell, where the increase in size or mass has the specific outcome of the progression of the organism over time from one condition to another.

nodes.label: cell growth
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cell growth as: The process in which a cell irreversibly increases in size over time by accretion and biosynthetic production of matter similar to that already present.

nodes.label: filamentous growth
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines filamentous growth as: The process in which a multicellular organism, a unicellular organism or a group of unicellular organisms grow in a threadlike, filamentous shape.

nodes.label: lateral growth
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines lateral growth as: Growth of a plant axis (shoot axis or root) that originates from a lateral meristem.

nodes.label: budding cell bud growth
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines budding cell bud growth as: The process in which the bud portion of a cell that reproduces by budding irreversibly increases in size over time by accretion and biosynthetic production of matter similar to that already present.

nodes.label: detection of stimulus
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines detection of stimulus as: The series of events in which a stimulus is received by a cell or organism and converted into a molecular signal.

nodes.label: immune response
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines immune response as: Any immune system process that functions in the calibrated response of an organism to a potential internal or invasive threat.

nodes.label: muscle adaptation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines muscle adaptation as: A process in which muscle adapts, with consequent modifications to structural and/or functional phenotypes, in response to a stimulus. Stimuli include contractile activity, loading conditions, substrate supply, and environmental factors. These adaptive events occur in both muscle fibers and associated structures (motoneurons and capillaries), and they involve alterations in regulatory mechanisms, contractile properties and metabolic capacities.

nodes.label: fusion of viral membrane with host outer nuclear membrane
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines fusion of viral membrane with host outer nuclear membrane as: Fusion of a viral primary envelope with the host outer nuclear membrane during nuclear egress. The transitory primary envelope is acquired by the virus as it buds at the inner nuclear membrane and gains access to the perinuclear space. This membrane is lost by fusing with the host outer nuclear membrane during nuclear exit.

nodes.label: latency-replication decision
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines latency-replication decision as: The process by which a virus switches on its replication cycle in an infected cell. The process is typically controlled by a genetic switch controlled by environmental factors such as cell type, cell shape, the availability of nutrients, superinfection or exposure of infected cells to UV or various chemical stimuli.

nodes.label: viral genome integration into host DNA
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral genome integration into host DNA as: The insertion into a host genome of viral DNA, usually by the action of an integrase enzyme. Once integrated, the provirus persists in the host cell and serves as a template for the transcription of viral genes and replication of the viral genome, leading to the production of new viruses.

nodes.label: permeabilization of host organelle membrane involved in viral entry into host cell
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines permeabilization of host organelle membrane involved in viral entry into host cell as: Induction of organellar membrane permeabilization triggered by an interaction between the host membrane and a membrane-penetration protein associated with a viral capsid. Results in release of the virus contents from an organelle into the host cell cytoplasm.

nodes.label: membrane fusion involved in viral entry into host cell
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines membrane fusion involved in viral entry into host cell as: Merging of the virion membrane and a host membrane (host plasma membrane or host organelle membrane) that is involved in the uptake of a virus into a host cell.

nodes.label: viral life cycle
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral life cycle as: A set of processes which all viruses follow to ensure survival; includes attachment and entry of the virus particle, decoding of genome information, translation of viral mRNA by host ribosomes, genome replication, and assembly and release of viral particles containing the genome.

nodes.label: viral genome replication
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral genome replication as: Any process involved directly in viral genome replication, including viral nucleotide metabolism.

nodes.label: viral tropism switching
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral tropism switching as: A process by which the range of hosts which a virus can bind and infect is changed. Examples include phages that switch between types of fibers via the action of a virally encoded invertase.

nodes.label: viral mRNA export from host cell nucleus
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral mRNA export from host cell nucleus as: The directed movement of intronless viral mRNA from the host nucleus to the cytoplasm for translation.

nodes.label: virus maturation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virus maturation as: The refolding and structural rearrangements of virion parts to transition from the intermediate virion to the more mature virion. Maturation usually involves proteolysis events and changes in the folding of the virion proteins. Can occur inside the host cell or after release.

nodes.label: IRES-dependent viral translational initiation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines IRES-dependent viral translational initiation as: Process by which viral mRNA translation is initiated, where a domain in the 5' untranslated region (UTR) of the viral mRNA called an internal ribosome entry site (IRES) binds the host 43S preinitiation complex, circumventing regular cap-dependent translation initiation.

nodes.label: viral capsid secondary envelopment
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral capsid secondary envelopment as: The process in which a capsid acquires another membrane envelope, subsequent to acquiring an initial membrane envelope.

nodes.label: viral translation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral translation as: A process by which viral mRNA is translated into viral protein, using the host cellular machinery.

nodes.label: ribosomal skipping
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ribosomal skipping as: A translation process in which a specific viral peptide prevents the ribosome from covalently linking a new inserted amino acid, and lets it continue translation, thereby cleaving the nascent protein while allowing translation to continue.

nodes.label: viral tail assembly
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral tail assembly as: The aggregation, arrangement and bonding together of a set of components to form a virus tail.

nodes.label: viral head-tail joining
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral head-tail joining as: Process by which virus heads and tails are attached to each other.

nodes.label: cap snatching
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines cap snatching as: A transcription initiation process during which a nucleotide sequence between 10 and 20 nucleotides in size is cleaved from the 5' end of host mRNAs by a viral RNA-dependent polymerase. The capped leader sequence obtained is subsequently used to prime transcription on the viral genome, which ultimately leads to the synthesis of capped, translatable viral mRNAs.

nodes.label: symbiont genome ejection through host cell envelope
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines symbiont genome ejection through host cell envelope as: Entry of a symbiont's genome into the host cell through the host cell envelope. Occurs in non-enveloped prokaryotic viruses. Caudovirales carry an ejection apparatus that can be long and contractile, long and noncontractile, or short, and is able to penetrate the host cell envelope to deliver the viral genome into the host cell cytoplasm.

nodes.label: exit of virus from host cell nucleus
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines exit of virus from host cell nucleus as: The directed movement of the viral genome or a viral particle out of the host cell nucleus.

nodes.label: transport of virus
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines transport of virus as: The directed movement of a virus, or part of a virus, into, out of, or within a host cell.

nodes.label: superinfection exclusion
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines superinfection exclusion as: The process by which a preexisting viral infection prevents a secondary infection with the same or a closely related virus. Typically some aspect of viral entry is inhibited, but post entry mechanisms have also been documented.

nodes.label: latent virus replication
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines latent virus replication as: Any process required for latent viral replication in a cell.

nodes.label: virion assembly
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virion assembly as: A late phase of the viral life cycle during which all the components necessary for the formation of a mature virion collect at a particular site in the cell and the basic structure of the virus particle is formed.

nodes.label: viral scaffold assembly and maintenance
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral scaffold assembly and maintenance as: The assembly and maintenance of the viral scaffold around which the viral capsid is constructed.

nodes.label: viral transcription
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral transcription as: The process by which a viral genome, or part of a viral genome, is transcribed within the host cell.

nodes.label: viral genome maturation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral genome maturation as: The processes involved in creating a mature, stable viral genome. Begins after genome replication with a newly synthesized nucleic acid and ends when the genome is ready to be packaged. Includes the addition of proteins to the newly synthesized genome, and DNA repair processes.

nodes.label: viral budding
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral budding as: A viral process by which enveloped viruses acquire a host-derived membrane enriched in viral proteins to form their external envelope. The process starts when nucleocapsids, assembled or in the process of being built, induce formation of a membrane curvature in the host plasma or organelle membrane and wrap up in the forming bud. The process ends when the bud is eventually pinched off by membrane scission to release the enveloped particle into the lumenal or extracellular space.

nodes.label: reorganization of host cellular membranes to establish sites of replication
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines reorganization of host cellular membranes to establish sites of replication as: A process in which a virus triggers host intracellular membranes to be reorganized, forming membranous webs, which are thought to be the site of replication or certain viruses, for example the HPV virus.

nodes.label: lysis of host organelle involved in viral entry into host cell
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines lysis of host organelle involved in viral entry into host cell as: The viral-induced lysis of an organelle (endosome, lysosome, or caveosome) that is involved in the uptake of a virus into a host cell. Occurs once the virus is within the organelle, and results in transfer of the viral contents from the organelle compartment into the cytoplasm.

nodes.label: virus baseplate assembly
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virus baseplate assembly as: The aggregation, arrangement and bonding together of a set of components to form a virus baseplate.

nodes.label: viral release from host cell
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral release from host cell as: The dissemination of mature viral particles from a host cell, e.g. by cell lysis or the budding of virus particles from the cell membrane.

nodes.label: virion maturation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virion maturation as: Maturation of a virion after separation from the host cell. Not all viruses mature after separation. In those that do, maturation typically involves rearangement and/or cleavage of viral proteins, resulting in the virion becoming competent for reinfection.

nodes.label: viral genome packaging
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral genome packaging as: The encapsulation of the viral genome within the capsid.

nodes.label: viral translational frameshifting
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral translational frameshifting as: A process which occurs during viral translation, which involves a translational recoding mechanism called programmed ribosomal frameshifting. This causes the ribosome to alter its reading of the mRNA to an a different open reading frame to produce alternate viral proteins.

nodes.label: viral protein processing
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral protein processing as: Any protein maturation process achieved by the cleavage of a peptide bond or bonds within a viral protein.

nodes.label: viral translational termination-reinitiation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral translational termination-reinitiation as: A process which occurs as part of viral mRNA translation which allows expression of a downstream open reading frame (ORF) in a dicistronic mRNA. In this process, ribosomes translate the upstream ORF but following termination, a proportion of 40S subunits remain tethered to the mRNA and go on to re-initiate translation at the start codon of the downstream ORF.

nodes.label: viral gene expression
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral gene expression as: A process by which a viral gene is converted into a mature gene product or products (proteins or RNA). This includes viral transcription, processing to produce a mature RNA product, and viral translation.

nodes.label: viral replication complex formation and maintenance
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral replication complex formation and maintenance as: The process of organizing and assembling viral replication proteins in preparation for viral replication.

nodes.label: virus tail fiber assembly
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines virus tail fiber assembly as: The aggregation, arrangement and bonding together of a set of components to form a virus tail fiber.

nodes.label: viral RNA editing
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral RNA editing as: The process by which bases in viral mRNA are chemically altered during viral transcription. This is usually the incorporation of 1 - 6 additional nucleotides, which shifts the reading frame, allowing the generation of different protein products or through a specific nucleotide change that eliminates the termination codon.

nodes.label: viral capsid assembly
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral capsid assembly as: The assembly of a virus capsid from its protein subunits.

nodes.label: viral genome circularization
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral genome circularization as: The circularization of a viral genome following infection of a host cell. This is common amongst bacterial viruses to protect the viral genome ends from nucleases, to convert the linear genome to an integrative precursor or to give rise to the replicative form of the genome. It can be mediated by covalent closure of the DNA sticky ends, recombinaison between redundant terminal sequences or via the binding of a protein at the viral DNA extremities.

nodes.label: release from viral latency
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines release from viral latency as: The process by which a virus begins to replicate following a latency replication decision (switch).

nodes.label: uncoating of virus
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines uncoating of virus as: The process by which an incoming virus is disassembled in the host cell to release a replication-competent viral genome.

nodes.label: viral latency
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines viral latency as: The process by which, after initial infection, a virus lies dormant within a cell and viral production ceases. The process ends when the virus switches from latency and starts to replicate.

nodes.label: multicellular organismal reproductive process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines multicellular organismal reproductive process as: The process, occurring above the cellular level, that is pertinent to the reproductive function of a multicellular organism. This includes the integrated processes at the level of tissues and organs.

nodes.label: fertilization
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines fertilization as: The union of gametes of opposite sexes during the process of sexual reproduction to form a zygote. It involves the fusion of the gametic nuclei (karyogamy) and cytoplasm (plasmogamy).

nodes.label: reproductive process in single-celled organism
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines reproductive process in single-celled organism as: A process, occurring at the cellular level, that is involved in the reproductive function of a single-celled organism.

nodes.label: premature acrosome loss
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines premature acrosome loss as: The discharge, by sperm, of a single, anterior secretory granule before the sperm reaches to the zona pellucida of the oocyte. The process begins with the fusion of the outer acrosomal membrane with the sperm plasma membrane and ends with the exocytosis of the acrosomal contents.

nodes.label: mating plug formation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines mating plug formation as: The deposition of a plug of sperm or other gelatinous material into the opening of the vulva by a male at the termination of copulation. Probably acts to prevent subsequent matings by other males.

nodes.label: sexual reproduction
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines sexual reproduction as: A type of reproduction that combines the genetic material of two gametes (such as a sperm or egg cell or fungal spores). The gametes have an haploid genome (with a single set of chromosomes, the product of a meiotic division) and combines with one another to produce a zygote (diploid).

nodes.label: ovulation cycle process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines ovulation cycle process as: A process involved in the sexual cycle seen in females, often with physiologic changes in the endometrium that recur at regular intervals during the reproductive years.

nodes.label: embryo implantation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines embryo implantation as: Attachment of the blastocyst to the uterine lining.

nodes.label: multi-organism reproductive process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines multi-organism reproductive process as: A biological process that directly contributes to the process of producing new individuals, involving another organism.

nodes.label: sperm motility
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines sperm motility as: Any process involved in the controlled movement of a sperm cell.

nodes.label: meiotic drive
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines meiotic drive as: A biological process that results in the unequal transmission of alleles, haplotypes, or chromosomes from a parental genome to gametes. In the absence of meiotic drive, the two copies of each gene or chromosome in a diploid organism are transmitted to offspring with equal probability, whereas meiotic drive results in overrepresentation of the driving allele among the surviving products of meiosis.

nodes.label: acrosome reaction
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines acrosome reaction as: The discharge, by sperm, of a single, anterior secretory granule following the sperm's attachment to the zona pellucida of the oocyte. The process begins with the fusion of the outer acrosomal membrane with the sperm plasma membrane and ends with the exocytosis of the acrosomal contents into the zona pellucida.

nodes.label: meiotic cell cycle
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines meiotic cell cycle as: Progression through the phases of the meiotic cell cycle, in which canonically a cell replicates to produce four offspring with half the chromosomal content of the progenitor cell via two nuclear divisions.

nodes.label: meiotic cell cycle process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines meiotic cell cycle process as: A process that is part of the meiotic cell cycle.

nodes.label: developmental process involved in reproduction
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines developmental process involved in reproduction as: A developmental process in which a progressive change in the state of some part of an organism, germline or somatic, specifically contributes to its ability to form offspring.

nodes.label: asexual reproduction
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines asexual reproduction as: A type of reproduction in which new individuals are produced from a single organism, either from an unfertilized egg or from a single cell or group of cells.

nodes.label: spore dispersal
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines spore dispersal as: Any process in which an organism disseminates its spores.

nodes.label: parasexual reproduction with cellular fusion
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines parasexual reproduction with cellular fusion as: A type of reproduction in which new individuals are produced from two individuals, with the fusion of two somatic cells.

nodes.label: antigen sampling in mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines antigen sampling in mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue as: The process of apical-to-basolateral delivery of soluble and particulate antigens to underlying mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue.

nodes.label: antigen processing and presentation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines antigen processing and presentation as: The process in which an antigen-presenting cell expresses antigen (peptide or lipid) on its cell surface in association with an MHC protein complex.

nodes.label: leukocyte homeostasis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines leukocyte homeostasis as: The process of regulating the proliferation and elimination of cells of the immune system such that the total number of cells of a particular cell type within a whole or part of an organism is stable over time in the absence of an outside stimulus.

nodes.label: tolerance induction
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines tolerance induction as: A process that directly activates any of the steps required for tolerance, a physiologic state in which the immune system does not react destructively against the components of an organism that harbors it or against antigens that are introduced to it.

nodes.label: B cell selection
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines B cell selection as: The process dependent upon B cell antigen receptor signaling in response to self or foreign antigen through which B cells are selected for survival.

nodes.label: activation of immune response
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines activation of immune response as: Any process that initiates an immune response.

nodes.label: leukocyte activation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines leukocyte activation as: A change in morphology and behavior of a leukocyte resulting from exposure to a specific antigen, mitogen, cytokine, cellular ligand, or soluble factor.

nodes.label: immune effector process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines immune effector process as: Any process of the immune system that executes a component of an immune response. An effector immune process takes place after its activation.

nodes.label: immunological memory process
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines immunological memory process as: Any process of the immune system that can contribute to the formation of immunological memory or an immune response based upon activation of immunological memory.

nodes.label: lymphocyte costimulation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines lymphocyte costimulation as: The process of providing, via surface-bound receptor-ligand pairs, a second, antigen-independent, signal in addition to that provided by the B- or T cell receptor to augment B- or T cell activation.

nodes.label: production of molecular mediator of immune response
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines production of molecular mediator of immune response as: The synthesis or release of any molecular mediator of the immune response, resulting in an increase in its intracellular or extracellular levels.

nodes.label: somatic diversification of immune receptors
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines somatic diversification of immune receptors as: The somatic process allowing for the production of immune receptors whose specificity is not encoded in the germline genomic sequences.

nodes.label: myeloid cell homeostasis
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines myeloid cell homeostasis as: The process of regulating the proliferation and elimination of myeloid cells such that the total number of myeloid cells within a whole or part of an organism is stable over time in the absence of an outside stimulus.

nodes.label: immune system development
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines immune system development as: The process whose specific outcome is the progression of an organismal system whose objective is to provide calibrated responses by an organism to a potential internal or invasive threat, over time, from its formation to the mature structure. A system is a regularly interacting or interdependent group of organs or tissues that work together to carry out a given biological process.

nodes.label: hemocyte differentiation
nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines hemocyte differentiation as: The process in which a relatively unspecialized cell acquires the characteristics of a mature hemocyte. Hemocytes are blood cells associated with a hemocoel (the cavity containing most of the major organs of the arthropod body) which are involved in defense and clotting of hemolymph, but not involved in transport of oxygen.

nodes.label: hemocyte proliferation
