nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ancient Central African as: Cultures and styles of Central Africa in ancient times.

nodes.label: Ancient Southern African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ancient Southern African as: Cultures and styles of southern Africa in ancient times.

nodes.label: ancient East African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ancient East African as: Cultures and styles of East Africa in ancient times.

nodes.label: Ancient North African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ancient North African as: Styles and cultures of North Africa in ancient times.

nodes.label: modern East African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines modern East African as: Styles and culture belonging to modern East Africa.

nodes.label: Southern African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Southern African as: Styles and cultures originating in the southernmost region of the African continent, comprising the modern countries of Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Swaziland, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. The island nation of Madagascar is excluded because of its distinct language and cultural heritage.

nodes.label: Eastern African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Eastern African as: Styles and cultures of the eastern area of Africa, traditionally divided into two parts: East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda) and the Horn of Africa (Somalia, Djibouti, Eritrea, and Ethiopia).

nodes.label: North African
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines North African as: Styles and cultures of the African peoples living in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, and Mauritania.

nodes.label: Pole Style
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Pole Style as: Style of African sculpture, typically elongated, severe, and abstract-looking.

nodes.label: Round Style
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Round Style as: Style of African sculpture, characteristically naturalistic, gentle, and organic, featuring rounded shapes, and giving the impression of flesh over the bone structure.

nodes.label: Turkestani
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Turkestani as: Culture and styles of historic Turkestan, a region in Central Asia inhabited by Turkic and other peoples.

nodes.label: West Turkestani
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines West Turkestani as: Refers to the culture and styles of West Turkestan, which covered present-day Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and the southern part of Kazakhstan.

nodes.label: Taiwanese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Taiwanese as: Nationality, styles, or culture of Taiwan, East Asia.

nodes.label: Afanasievo
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Afanasievo as: Refers to the Neolithic culture established in the slopes of the Afanasyevskaya Mountains from the 2nd millennium BCE. Sites have revealed tombs marked with stone circles symbolizing the Sun God, later ones took the form of barrows or large mounds. Pottery in earlier graves consisted of elongated, spherical vessels with herringbone patterns, while later pottery was flat-bottomed.

nodes.label: Altai
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Altai as: Style and culture of the mountain range running along border shared by China and Mongolia.

nodes.label: Andronovo
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Andronovo as: Refers to the Neolithic culture established in the steppes of the Minusinsk basin during the 2nd and 1st millennia BCE. Sites have revealed earth houses designed for permanent habitation, with hearths for heating purposes and cooking. Bronze objects were also numerous, and workshops existed for working copper.

nodes.label: Karasuk
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Karasuk as: Refers to the Iron Age culture established in the Minusinsk basin on the Yenisey River from about 1200 BCE to about 70 BCE. Sites have revealed elbow-shaped knifes related to those used between the 14th and 11th centuries BCE in China during the Shang Period. Also notable are pillars with stylized ram heads or human figures.

nodes.label: Okunev
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Okunev as: Refers to the Eneolithic culture established in the steppes of the Minusinsk basin by Mongoloid peoples probably of Northern Siberian descent, from the beginning of the 2nd millennium BCE. Tombs have revealed a variety of stone sculptures.

nodes.label: Siberian Arctic Native styles
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Siberian Arctic Native styles as: Styles belonging to Siberian Arctic Native cultures.

nodes.label: Tashtyk
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Tashtyk as: Refers to the Eneolithic culture established in the Minusinsk Basin between the 1st century BCE and the 5th century CE. Notable artifacts from the period include examples of the Scynthian-Siberian Animal style on bronze and gold, and clay funeral masks portraying faces with a two-color decoration.

nodes.label: Tungus
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Tungus as: Culture and style of the indigenous Tungusic people native to the vast subarctic boreal forests (taiga) of Siberia and the Russian Far East, as well as parts of northern China and Mongolia.

nodes.label: Assamese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Assamese as: The Assamese are a major ethnic group of approximately 19.5 million people centered in the Indian state of Assam in northeastern India, speaking Assamese, the easternmost Indo-Aryan language with over 15 million native speakers. Their culture developed largely in isolation along the Brahmaputra River valley, shaped by centuries of interaction with neighboring Tibeto-Burman peoples, Tibetan influences, and the Ahom kingdom established by Tai invaders in 1229. Predominantly Hindu with animist traditions, the Assamese reflect a diverse heritage of Aryan, Ahom, and indigenous influences, and their language has historically served as a regional lingua franca across parts of northeastern India.

nodes.label: Bangladeshi
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Bangladeshi as: The nationality, style, or culture of Bangladesh, located at the northeast corner of the Indian subcontinent.

nodes.label: Indic
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Indic as: Culture and style of a diverse ethnolinguistic collection of peoples predominantly found in South Asia who speak languages belonging to the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European family. As they settled the fertile Indus and Gangetic plains, their semi-nomadic pastoral lifestyle transitioned into intensive iron-age agriculture. They brought with them horses, spoked-wheel chariots, and a highly structured spiritual tradition.

nodes.label: Magars
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Magars as: The Magars are a Sino-Tibetan/Tibeto-Burman ethnic group native primarily to west-central Nepal, where they represent approximately 6.9% of the national population, with additional communities in northern India, Bhutan, Bangladesh, and diaspora populations worldwide. Their traditional homeland, historically known as Magarat, centered on the Palpa region west of the Gandaki River and was organized into confederations of twelve and eighteen Magar kingdoms during the medieval period. The Magars speak the Magar language (Magar Kura) in two major dialectal groups, practice a blend of Tibetan Buddhism, Hinduism, and shamanistic traditions, and are historically renowned for their service in Gurkha military regiments.

nodes.label: Pakistani
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Pakistani as: Refers to the style and culture of modern Pakistan.

nodes.label: Sri Lankan
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Sri Lankan as: Culture and style of an Indo-Aryan ethnic group native to the island country of Sri Lanka. They possess a 2,500-year written history characterized by grand ancient kingdoms, pioneering hydraulic engineering, and a foundational role in the preservation of Theravada Buddhism.

nodes.label: Akha
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Akha as: The Akha are an ethnic group inhabiting mountainous regions of Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, and China's Yunnan Province, with approximately 80,000 now residing in northern Thailand following migrations that intensified during the 20th century due to civil conflicts. They speak Akha, a Loloish language within the Tibeto-Burman family that is closely related to Lisu. Historical evidence suggests the Akha may have ruled the Baoshan and Tengchong plains in Yunnan prior to the Ming dynasty invasion of 1644.

nodes.label: Batak
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Batak as: The Batak are a collective term for closely related Austronesian ethnic groups predominantly found in North Sumatra and adjacent provinces of Indonesia, who speak related Batak languages and share cultural traditions. The term encompasses six main subgroups—the Toba, Karo, Simalungun, Pakpak-Dairi, Angkola, and Mandailing—as well as other related ethnic groups with distinct languages and traditional customs (adat). With an estimated population of 6 million centered around Lake Toba, the Batak maintain indigenous writing systems (surat Batak) and diverse religious practices including Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, and syncretic traditions such as Malim.

nodes.label: Brao
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Brao as: The Brao are a Mon-Khmer language-speaking ethnic group of approximately 60,000 people divided into multiple subgroups, primarily residing in the southern Lao provinces of Champasak and Attapeu, the northeastern Cambodian provinces of Ratanakiri and Stung Treng, and a single village in Vietnam's Central Highlands. Historically inhabiting upland forested landscapes where they practiced swidden agriculture as their main livelihood, the Brao have experienced significant displacement as many communities in both Laos and Cambodia have been variously manipulated, coerced, or forced to resettle to lowland areas and adopt wet rice cultivation. This resettlement represents a major disruption to traditional Brao land use patterns and subsistence practices that were historically centered on upland forest environments.

nodes.label: Burmese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Burmese as: Refers generally to the ethnic cultures of the region corresponding to modern Myanmar located in the western region of mainland Southeast Asia. Refers specifically to the style and period of the British colonial occupation from 1885 to 1948. Art in the region reveals bas-relief and monumental stone sculptures of Buddhist iconography and some British colonial influences.

nodes.label: Cambodian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Cambodian as: Nationality, culture, or style of Cambodia, located in the southern portion of the Indochina Peninsula in Southeast Asia. Arts and crafts of the region reveal Indian and other regional influences through various sculptures of wood and stone, lapidary pieces comprised of silver, gold, and ivory, and silk sheath pieces in various luxurious hues of red, blue, and gold.

nodes.label: Dayak
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Dayak as: The Dayak are indigenous Austronesian ethnic groups native to Borneo, comprising over 200 distinct riverine and hill-dwelling communities located principally in the central and southern interior of the island, each with its own dialect, customs, laws, territory, and culture. While these diverse groups share common distinguishing cultural traits, they maintain distinct identities and traditions. Historically practicing animist beliefs (Kaharingan and Folk Hinduism), the Dayak have undergone significant religious transformation since the 19th century, with mass conversions to Christianity and Islam.

nodes.label: Hmong
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Hmong as: Refers to the style and culture of the Hmong people centralized in scattered areas throughout China, Vietnam, Laos, and Thailand. Artistic production in this style features predominantly silver jewelry designs ranging from sliver chain necklaces with lock-shaped pendants attached to neck-rings, large collar necklaces covering the entire chest-area, heavy and narrow bracelets, to circle earrings that surround the ear, widening from narrow ends to a broad center, with pointed pendants hanging from tiny chains. Textile styles feature batik production characterized by geometric patterns on hemp and cotton, appliqué and reverse appliqué in bold colors, cold-dyed indigo, specific symbolic embroidery designs such as mustard blossom, cucumber seed, tiger teeth, and eye of the peacock, elaborate needlework, silk cocoon fibers, and flower and story cloth panel designs depicting village life, shaman's séances, legends and warfare.

nodes.label: Indochinese
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Indochinese as: Nationality and culture of the region between India and China, the areas of the current nations Burma, Kampuchea (Cambodia), Laos, Thailand, Vietnam and Malaysia.

nodes.label: Indonesian
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Indonesian as: Refers to the cultures and styles of Indonesia, reflecting the blend of various regional cultures from the Southeast Asian mainland and Oceania. The style is generally driven by the philosophies of Buddhism, Hinduism, and Islam. Sculptural production in the region generally features megalithic monuments such as menhirs, dolmens, stone sarcophagi, terraced burial mounds, large stones carved into the shape of animals and humans, and stone skull troughs. Early styles of sculpture in the region feature smooth planes, convexity, impassive expressions, and lack of movement. Ornamental works from this region imitate Chinese Chou and pre-Han works and feature bronze drums with molded flanges and relief ornamentation consisting of stylized masks with ear piercings. Indian-influenced works feature intricate bronze Buddhas and bodhisattvas. In architecture, the style features temple complexes known as tjandis and candis.

nodes.label: Jarai
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Jarai as: The Jarai (or Dega) are an Austronesian indigenous people inhabiting Vietnam's Central Highlands and Cambodia's Ratanakiri Province, with diaspora communities in the United States following their collaboration with US forces during the Vietnam War. Speaking a Malayo-Polynesian language related to Cham and other Pacific Island languages, the approximately 332,558 Jarai constitute the largest Montagnard ethnic group and comprise 23% of Ratanakiri's population. While Cambodian and Vietnamese Jarai communities maintain shared cultural traditions and close interchange, their languages have diverged due to respective Khmer and Vietnamese linguistic influences, with only the Vietnamese Jarai possessing a standardized Latin script writing system.

nodes.label: Kachin
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Kachin as: Culture of the tribal Tibeto-Burman ethnic group inhabiting parts of northeastern Myanmar (Burma) and contiguous areas of India (Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland) and China (Yunnan).

nodes.label: African (general, continental cultures)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines African (general, continental cultures) as: Refers to the cultures of the continent of Africa, which is bounded by the Atlantic Ocean, the Indian Ocean, and the Mediterranean Sea.

nodes.label: Siberian (culture or style)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Siberian (culture or style) as: Style and culture of Siberia, particularly to that of any of the large number of small ethnic groups living in Siberia. Most engage either in reindeer herding or fishing, while some also hunt furbearing animals or farm and raise horses or cattle.

nodes.label: architecture (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines architecture (discipline) as: The art or science of designing and building structures, especially habitable structures, in accordance with principles determined by aesthetic and practical or material considerations. For a general term for the actual structures or parts of structures that were made by human beings, see "architecture (object genre)."

nodes.label: visual arts (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines visual arts (discipline) as: Discipline concerning physical objects that are meant to be perceived primarily through the sense of sight, were created by the use of skill and imagination, and possess an aesthetic that is valued and of a quality and type that would be collected by art museums or private collectors.

nodes.label: arts (broad discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines arts (broad discipline) as: Refers broadly to the areas of activity that encompass both performing and visual arts. With reference more narrowly to the fine arts or the fine and decorative arts together, see "art."

nodes.label: design (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines design (discipline) as: Discipline comprising the creation of conceptual schemes for the organization or appearance of graphic works, objects, structures, or systems.

nodes.label: grammar (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines grammar (discipline) as: The study of the rules of a language governing the sounds, words, sentences, and other elements, including their structure, combination, and interpretation.

nodes.label: religion (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religion (discipline) as: Study of religious beliefs and traditions in human life and culture from the perspective of the humanistic disciplines.

nodes.label: <religion and related disciplines>
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines <religion and related disciplines> as: The discipline of religion and closely related disciplines.

nodes.label: Associated Concepts
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Associated Concepts as: The Associated Concepts hierarchy contains terms for concepts and phenomena relating to a wide range of topics, including topics not directly related to art, for example philosophical concepts. Relation to other hierarchies: Terms for branches of learning and areas of specialization, as well as professions and professional specialties, (e.g., "history") are found in the Disciplines hierarchy, while concepts associated with these disciplines (e.g., "positivism ") appear here. Terms for styles and for art and architecture movements (e.g., "Neoclassical," "Impressionist") are found in the Styles and Periods hierarchy, while forms of expression (e.g., "abstraction") and broad categories of art and architecture that are not specific to a given people or period (e.g., "organic architecture," "street art") are here.

nodes.label: <linguistics and related disciplines>
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines <linguistics and related disciplines> as: The discipline of linguistics and other disciplines related to it.

nodes.label: <religions and religious concepts>
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines <religions and religious concepts> as: Religions and concepts related to religions.

nodes.label: music (performing arts genre)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines music (performing arts genre) as: Performing arts genre having to do with the combining of vocal or instrumental sounds in measured time to communicate emotions, ideas, or states of mind, usually according to cultural standards of rhythm, melody, and, in most Western music, harmony.

nodes.label: performing arts (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines performing arts (discipline) as: Disciplines concerning arts that depend upon performances presented to the attention of observers through the live or recorded actions of the artists, such as actors, musicians, poets, etc.

nodes.label: music (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines music (discipline) as: The discipline of combining vocal or instrumental sounds to produce beauty of form, harmony, melody, rhythm, expressive content, etc.; musical composition, performance, analysis, etc., as a subject of study; the occupation or profession of musicians.

nodes.label: ethics (philosophical concept)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines ethics (philosophical concept) as: System of moral principles or rules of conduct for voluntary human action. For the branch of philosophy that studies these principles and rules, with respect to the rightness or wrongness of certain human actions, and the goodness or badness of the motives and ends of such actions, use "ethics (philosophy)."

nodes.label: dance (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines dance (discipline) as: Discipline involving the study of dancing and movement, including performance.

nodes.label: photography (discipline)
nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines photography (discipline) as: The dedicated practice of making photographs as an applied art.

nodes.label: Abstract algebra
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Abstract algebra", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, more specifically algebra, abstract algebra or modern algebra is the study of algebraic structures, which are sets with specific operations acting on their elements.

nodes.label: General topology
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "General topology", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, general topology (or point set topology) is the branch of topology that deals with the basic set-theoretic definitions and constructions used in topology.

nodes.label: Algebraic topology
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Algebraic topology", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Algebraic topology is a branch of mathematics that uses tools from abstract algebra to study topological spaces.

nodes.label: Complex analysis
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Complex analysis", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Complex analysis, traditionally known as the theory of functions of a complex variable, is the branch of mathematical analysis that studies complex-valued functions of one or more complex variables.

nodes.label: Functional analysis
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Functional analysis", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Functional analysis is a branch of mathematical analysis, the core of which is formed by the study of vector spaces endowed with some kind of limit-related structure (for example, inner product, norm, or topology) and the linear functions defined on these spaces and suitably respecting these structures.

nodes.label: Measure (mathematics)
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Measure (mathematics)", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, the concept of a measure is a generalization and formalization of geometrical measures (length, area, volume) and other common notions, such as magnitude, mass, and probability of events.

nodes.label: Combinatorics
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Combinatorics", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Combinatorics is an area of mathematics primarily concerned with counting, both as a means and as an end to obtaining results, and certain properties of finite structures.

nodes.label: Differential geometry
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Differential geometry", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Differential geometry is a mathematical discipline that studies the geometry of smooth shapes and smooth spaces, otherwise known as smooth manifolds.

nodes.label: Euclidean geometry
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Euclidean geometry", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Euclidean geometry is a mathematical system attributed to Euclid, an ancient Greek mathematician, which he described in his textbook on geometry, Elements.

nodes.label: Probability theory
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Probability theory", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Probability theory or probability calculus is the branch of mathematics concerned with probability.

nodes.label: Order theory
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Order theory", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Order theory is a branch of mathematics that investigates the intuitive notion of order using binary relations.

nodes.label: Mathematical logic
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Mathematical logic", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Mathematical logic is the study of formal logic within mathematics.

nodes.label: Mathematical analysis
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Mathematical analysis", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Mathematical analysis is the branch of mathematics that studies functions, spaces, and operators through methods of approximation and convergence.

nodes.label: Convergence space
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Convergence space", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, a convergence space, also called a generalized convergence, is a set together with a relation called a convergence that satisfies certain properties relating elements of X with the family of filters on X. Convergence spaces generalize the notions of convergence that are found in point-set topology, including metric convergence and uniform convergence.

nodes.label: Dynamical system
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Dynamical system", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, a dynamical system is a system in which a function describes the time dependence of a point in an ambient space, such as in a parametric curve.

nodes.label: Numerical analysis
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Numerical analysis", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Numerical analysis is the study of algorithms for the problems of continuous mathematics.

nodes.label: Module (mathematics)
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Module (mathematics)", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, a module is a generalization of the notion of vector space in which the field of scalars is replaced by a (not necessarily commutative) ring.

nodes.label: Prime number
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Prime number", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: A prime number (or a prime) is a natural number greater than 1 that is not a product of two smaller natural numbers.

nodes.label: Antoine's necklace
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Antoine's necklace", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, Antoine's necklace is a topological embedding of the Cantor set in 3-dimensional Euclidean space, whose complement is not simply connected.

nodes.label: Abel's binomial theorem
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Abel's binomial theorem", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Abel's binomial theorem, named after Niels Henrik Abel, is a mathematical identity involving sums of binomial coefficients.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Abel's binomial theorem

nodes.label: Alexander's subbase lemma
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Alexander's subbase lemma", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, specifically topology, Alexander's subbase lemma states that for a topological space to be a compact, it is necessary and sufficient that each open cover of the space consisting of sets in a (fixed) subbase has a finite subcover.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Alexander's subbase lemma

nodes.label: Calculus
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Calculus", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Calculus is the branch of mathematics that studies continuous change, and is the principal precursor of modern mathematical analysis.

nodes.label: Finite model theory
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Finite model theory", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Finite model theory is a subarea of model theory.

nodes.label: Condensed detachment

nodes.label: Harmonic analysis
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Harmonic analysis", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Harmonic analysis is an area of mathematical analysis that emerged from the study of harmonic functions, and especially their boundary behavior.

nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Homological algebra", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Homological algebra is the branch of mathematics that studies homology in a general algebraic setting.

nodes.label: Combinatorial principles
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Combinatorial principles", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In proving results in combinatorics several useful combinatorial rules or combinatorial principles are commonly recognized and used.

nodes.label: Geometric analysis
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Geometric analysis", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Geometric analysis is a mathematical discipline where tools from differential equations, especially elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs), are used to establish new results in differential geometry and differential topology.

nodes.label: Arens–Fort space
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Arens–Fort space", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, the Arens–Fort space is a special example in the theory of topological spaces, named for Richard Friederich Arens and M. K. Fort, Jr.

nodes.label: Abel's irreducibility theorem
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Abel's irreducibility theorem", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, Abel's irreducibility theorem, a field theory result described in 1829 by Niels Henrik Abel, asserts that if f(x) is a polynomial over a field F that shares a root with a polynomial g(x) that is irreducible over F, then every root of g(x) is a root of f(x).

nodes.label: Amalgamation property

nodes.label: Analytic proof
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Analytic proof", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, an analytic proof is a proof of a theorem in analysis that only makes use of methods from analysis, and that does not predominantly make use of algebraic or geometrical methods.

nodes.label: Affine plank problem
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Affine plank problem", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, the affine plank problem is an open question in convex geometry posed by Thøger Bang in 1951 as a strengthening of Tarski's plank problem.

nodes.label: Floquet theory

nodes.label: Bachmann–Howard ordinal
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Bachmann–Howard ordinal", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, the Bachmann–Howard ordinal (also known as the Howard ordinal, or Howard–Bachmann ordinal) is a large countable ordinal.

nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Addition principle", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In combinatorics, the addition principle or rule of sum is a basic counting principle.

nodes.label: Consensus dynamics
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Consensus dynamics", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Consensus dynamics, also known as agreement dynamics, is an area of research at the intersection of systems theory and graph theory.

nodes.label: Affine connection
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Affine connection", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In differential geometry, an affine connection is a geometric object on a smooth manifold which connects nearby tangent spaces, so it permits tangent vector fields to be differentiated as if they were functions on the manifold with values in a fixed vector space.

nodes.label: Carlyle circle
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Carlyle circle", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, a Carlyle circle is a certain circle in a coordinate plane associated with a quadratic equation; it is named after Thomas Carlyle.

nodes.label: Carré du champ operator
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Carré du champ operator", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The carré du champ operator (French for square of a field operator) is a bilinear, symmetric operator from analysis and probability theory.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Carré du champ operator

nodes.label: Accessible quasi-category
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Accessible quasi-category", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, especially category theory, an accessible quasi-category is a quasi-category in which each object is an ind-object on some small quasi-category.

nodes.label: Breather surface
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Breather surface", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In differential geometry, a breather surface is a one-parameter family of mathematical surfaces which correspond to breather solutions of the sine-Gordon equation, a differential equation appearing in theoretical physics.

nodes.label: Dominance order
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Dominance order", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In discrete mathematics, dominance order (synonyms: dominance ordering, majorization order, natural ordering) is a partial order on the set of partitions of a positive integer n that plays an important role in algebraic combinatorics and representation theory, especially in the context of symmetric functions and representation theory of the symmetric group.

nodes.label: Derivative of the exponential map
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Derivative of the exponential map", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In the theory of Lie groups, the exponential map is a map from the Lie algebra g of a Lie group G into G. In case G is a matrix Lie group, the exponential map reduces to the matrix exponential.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Derivative of the exponential map

nodes.label: Arithmetico-geometric sequence
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Arithmetico-geometric sequence", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, an arithmetico-geometric sequence is the result of element-by-element multiplication of the elements of a geometric progression with the corresponding elements of an arithmetic progression.

nodes.label: Hilbert–Burch theorem
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Hilbert–Burch theorem", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, the Hilbert–Burch theorem describes the structure of some free resolutions of a quotient of a local or graded ring in the case that the quotient has projective dimension 2.

nodes.label: Cyclic surgery theorem
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Cyclic surgery theorem", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In three-dimensional topology, a branch of mathematics, the cyclic surgery theorem states that, for a compact, connected, orientable, irreducible three-manifold M whose boundary is a torus T, if M is not a Seifert-fibered space and r,s are slopes on T such that their Dehn fillings have cyclic fundamental group, then the distance between r and s (the minimal number of times that two simple closed curves in T representing r and s must intersect) is at most 1.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Cyclic surgery theorem

nodes.label: Furstenberg boundary
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Furstenberg boundary", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, specifically harmonic analysis and probability theory, the Furstenberg boundary is a notion of boundary associated with a group.

nodes.label: Chain complex
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Chain complex", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, a chain complex is an algebraic structure that consists of a sequence of abelian groups (or modules) and a sequence of homomorphisms between consecutive groups such that the image of each homomorphism is contained in the kernel of the next.

nodes.label: Convex polygon
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Convex polygon", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In geometry, a convex polygon is a polygon that is the boundary of a convex set.

nodes.label: Alexander duality
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Alexander duality", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, Alexander duality refers to a duality theory initiated by a result of J. W. Alexander in 1915, and subsequently further developed, particularly by Pavel Alexandrov and Lev Pontryagin.

nodes.label: Amicable triple
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Amicable triple", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, an amicable triple is a set of three different numbers so related that the restricted sum of the divisors of each is equal to the sum of the other two numbers.

nodes.label: Associative property
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Associative property", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, the associative property is a property of some binary operations that rearranging the parentheses in an expression will not change the result.

nodes.label: Cantor function
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Cantor function", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, the Cantor function is an example of a function that is continuous, but not absolutely continuous.

nodes.label: Casey's theorem
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Casey's theorem", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, Casey's theorem, also known as the generalized Ptolemy's theorem, is a theorem in Euclidean geometry named after the Irish mathematician John Casey.

nodes.label: Betweenness problem
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Betweenness problem", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Betweenness is an algorithmic problem in order theory about ordering a collection of items subject to constraints that some items must be placed between others.

nodes.label: Dual lattice
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Dual lattice", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In the theory of lattices, the dual lattice is a construction analogous to that of a dual vector space.

nodes.label: Bitopological space
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Bitopological space", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, a bitopological space is a set endowed with two topologies.

nodes.label: Algebraic cycle
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Algebraic cycle", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, an algebraic cycle on an algebraic variety V is a formal linear combination of subvarieties of V. These are the part of the algebraic topology of V that is directly accessible by algebraic methods.

nodes.label: Autonomous system (mathematics)
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Autonomous system (mathematics)", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, an autonomous system or autonomous differential equation is a system of ordinary differential equations which does not explicitly depend on the independent variable.

nodes.label: Approximation error
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Approximation error", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The approximation error in a given data value represents the significant discrepancy that arises when an exact, true value is compared against some approximation derived for it.

nodes.label: Angelescu polynomials
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Angelescu polynomials", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, the Angelescu polynomials πn(x) are a series of polynomials generalizing the Laguerre polynomials introduced by Aurel Angelescu.

nodes.label: Automatic sequence
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Automatic sequence", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics and theoretical computer science, an automatic sequence (also called a k-automatic sequence or a k-recognizable sequence when one wants to indicate that the base of the numerals used is k) is an infinite sequence of terms characterized by a finite automaton.

nodes.label: Hochster–Roberts theorem
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Hochster–Roberts theorem", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In algebra, the Hochster–Roberts theorem, introduced by Melvin Hochster and Joel L. Roberts in 1974, states that rings of invariants of linearly reductive groups acting on regular rings are Cohen–Macaulay.

nodes.label: Catalan's conjecture
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Catalan's conjecture", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Catalan's conjecture (or Mihăilescu's theorem) is a theorem in number theory that was conjectured by the mathematician Eugène Charles Catalan in 1842 and proven in 2002 by Preda Mihăilescu at Paderborn University.

nodes.label: Differential (mathematics)
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Differential (mathematics)", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, differential refers to several related notions derived from the early days of calculus, put on a rigorous footing, such as infinitesimal differences and the derivatives of functions.

nodes.label: Elementary class
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Elementary class", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In model theory, a branch of mathematical logic, an elementary class (or axiomatizable class) is a class consisting of all structures satisfying a fixed first-order theory.

nodes.label: Chirp Z-transform
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Chirp Z-transform", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: The chirp Z-transform (CZT) is a generalization of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT).

nodes.label: Gelfand pair

nodes.label: Vietoris–Rips filtration
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Vietoris–Rips filtration", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In topological data analysis, the Vietoris–Rips filtration (sometimes shortened to "Rips filtration") is the collection of nested Vietoris–Rips complexes on a metric space created by taking the sequence of Vietoris–Rips complexes over an increasing scale parameter.

nodes.label: Arithmetic derivative
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Arithmetic derivative", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In number theory, the Lagarias arithmetic derivative or number derivative is a function defined for integers, based on prime factorization, by analogy with the product rule for the derivative of a function that is used in mathematical analysis.

nodes.label: Bounded variation
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Bounded variation", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematical analysis, a function of bounded variation, also known as BV function, is a real-valued function whose total variation is bounded (finite): the graph of a function having this property is well behaved in a precise sense.

nodes.label: Asymptotic geometry
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Asymptotic geometry", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Asymptotic geometry, also known as asymptotic geometric analysis or high-dimensional geometry, is a field of mathematics that investigates the geometric properties of finite-dimensional objects, such as convex bodies and normed spaces, as the dimension tends to infinity.

nodes.label: Cantor set
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Cantor set", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, the Cantor set is a self-similar set of points lying on a single line segment that has a number of unintuitive properties.

nodes.label: Cauchy's theorem (geometry)
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Cauchy's theorem (geometry)", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Cauchy's theorem is a theorem in geometry, named after Augustin Cauchy.

nodes.label: Boolean prime ideal theorem
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Boolean prime ideal theorem", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, the Boolean prime ideal theorem states that ideals in a Boolean algebra can be extended to prime ideals.

nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Bounding point", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In functional analysis, a branch of mathematics, a bounding point of a subset of a vector space is a conceptual extension of the boundary of a set.

nodes.label: Borel set
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Borel set", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, the Borel sets of a topological space are a particular class of "well-behaved" subsets of that space.

nodes.label: Approximation theory
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Approximation theory", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, approximation theory is concerned with how functions can best be approximated with simpler functions, and with quantitatively characterizing the errors introduced thereby.

nodes.label: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the second derivative
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the second derivative", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Explicit formulas for eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the second derivative with different boundary conditions are provided both for the continuous and discrete cases.

nodes.label: Baire space (set theory)

nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Excluded point topology", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, the excluded point topology is a topology where exclusion of a particular point defines openness.

nodes.label: Dialectica interpretation

nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Chirplet transform", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In signal processing, the chirplet transform is an inner product of an input signal with a family of analysis primitives called chirplets.

nodes.label: Group algebra of a locally compact group
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Group algebra of a locally compact group", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In functional analysis and related areas of mathematics, the group algebra is any of various constructions to assign to a locally compact group an operator algebra (or more generally a Banach algebra), such that representations of the algebra are related to representations of the group.

nodes.label: Cartan decomposition

nodes.label: Convex set
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Convex set", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In geometry, a set of points is convex if it contains every line segment between two points in the set.

nodes.label: Automorphisms of the symmetric and alternating groups
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Automorphisms of the symmetric and alternating groups", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In group theory, a branch of mathematics, the automorphisms and outer automorphisms of the symmetric groups and alternating groups are both standard examples of these automorphisms, and objects of study in their own right, particularly the exceptional outer automorphism of S6, the symmetric group on 6 elements.

nodes.label: Càdlàg

nodes.label: Bicoherence

nodes.label: Arc-length method

nodes.label: Countably generated module
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Countably generated module", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, a module over a (not necessarily commutative) ring is countably generated if it is generated as a module by a countable subset.

nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Freivalds' algorithm", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Freivalds' algorithm (named after Rūsiņš Mārtiņš Freivalds) is a probabilistic randomized algorithm used to verify matrix multiplication.

nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Ax–Grothendieck theorem", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, the Ax–Grothendieck theorem is a result about injectivity and surjectivity of polynomials that was proved independently by James Ax and Alexander Grothendieck.

nodes.label: Ban number

nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Fréchet manifold", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, in particular in nonlinear analysis, a Fréchet manifold is a topological space modeled on a Fréchet space in much the same way as a manifold is modeled on a Euclidean space.

nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Jacobson–Bourbaki theorem", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In algebra, the Jacobson–Bourbaki theorem is a theorem used to extend Galois theory to field extensions that need not be separable.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Gauss's lemma (Riemannian geometry)

nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Dirichlet average", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: Dirichlet averages are averages of functions under the Dirichlet distribution.

nodes.label: Monotone convergence theorem
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Monotone convergence theorem", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In real analysis, the monotone convergence theorem is any of a number of related theorems proving, under certain conditions, the convergence of monotonic sequences, i.e. sequences that are non-increasing, or non-decreasing.

sources.title: English Wikipedia article: Monotone convergence theorem

nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Convex space", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, a convex space (or barycentric algebra) is a space in which it is possible to take convex combinations of any finite set of points.

nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "(B, N) pair", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, a (B, N) pair is a structure on groups of Lie type that allows one to give uniform proofs of many results, instead of giving a large number of case-by-case proofs.

nodes.label: Basis (linear algebra)
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Basis (linear algebra)", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, a set B of elements of a vector space V is called a basis (pl.: bases) if every element of V can be written in a unique way as a finite linear combination of elements of B. nodes.label: Approximate fibration
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Approximate fibration", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In algebraic topology, a branch of mathematics, an approximate fibration is a sort of fibration such that the homotopy lifting property holds only approximately.

nodes.label: Alignments of random points

nodes.label: Chvátal–Sankoff constants
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Chvátal–Sankoff constants", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, the Chvátal–Sankoff constants are mathematical constants that describe the lengths of longest common subsequences of random strings.

nodes.label: Applied category theory

nodes.label: Beta-model

nodes.label: Bell polynomials
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Bell polynomials", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In combinatorial mathematics, the Bell polynomials, named in honor of Eric Temple Bell, are used in the study of set partitions.

nodes.label: Beatty sequence
nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Beatty sequence", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, a Beatty sequence (or homogeneous Beatty sequence) is the sequence of integers found by taking the floor of the positive multiples of an irrational number that is greater than one.

nodes.label: Fort space

nodes.label: Artinian ring

nodes.summary: English Wikipedia (article "Basis function", CC BY-SA 4.0) states: In mathematics, a basis function is an element of a particular basis for a function space.

support.quote:
Title:
A Spin Entanglement Witness for Quantum Gravity
[Submitted on 19 Jul 2017]

Here, we introduce an idea for such a test based on the principle that two objects cannot be entangled without a quantum mediator. We show that despite the weakness of gravity, the phase evolution induced by the gravitational interaction of two micron size test masses in adjacent matter-wave interferometers can detectably entangle them even when they are placed far apart enough to keep Casimir-Polder forces at bay. We provide a prescription for witnessing this entanglement, which certifies gravity as a quantum coherent mediator, through simple correlation measurements between two spins: one embedded in each test mass.

Subjects:
Quantum Physics (quant-ph)
; General Relativity and Quantum Cosmology (gr-qc); High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

Title:
Dark Matter Search Results from 4.2 Tonne-Years of Exposure of the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) Experiment

We report results of a search for nuclear recoils induced by weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) dark matter using the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) two-phase xenon time projection chamber. This analysis uses a total exposure of $4.2\pm0.1$ tonne-years from 280 live days of LZ operation, of which $3.3\pm0.1$ tonne-years and 220 live days are new.
After removal of artificial signal-like events injected into the data set to mitigate analyzer bias, we find no evidence for an excess over expected backgrounds.

Subjects:
High Energy Physics - Experiment (hep-ex)

canonical_record.label: Dresser siliceous ridges interpreted as sinter terracettes

sources.title: Earliest signs of life on land preserved in ca. 3.5 Ga hot spring deposits

assertions.statement: At Dresser locality 1S, the authors interpret convex siliceous ridges above stratiform geyserite as resembling mid- to distal-apron hot-spring sinter terracettes.

scope.population: Stratiform geyserite and overlying siliceous ridge unit at Dresser locality 1S
scope.assumptions: Resemblance in primary porosity and microtextures to younger hot-spring terracettes
scope.uncertainty: Analogue-based interpretation, not direct proof of microbial construction
scope.quantifiers: 3 cm thick unit; ridges approximately 1 cm across and under 2 cm high

support.quote: stratiform geyserite is overlain by a 3 cm thick unit composed of siliceous, millimetre-thin laminae that form ∼1 cm diameter, low-amplitude (<2 cm), asymmetrical convex ridges

The convex laminae in cross-section resemble sinter terracettes (smaller-scale subsets within sinter terraces) from the mid- to distal-apron facies of hot springs, displaying the primary porosity and microtextures comparable with more recent, microbially derived examples

scope.uncertainty: Proposed reinterpretation of at least some masses; no claim applying to all barite occurrences
scope.quantifiers: At least some, not all, masses

support.quote: However, new observations suggest that at least some of these barite masses represent the mineralized remnants of terrestrial hot spring pools and associated shallow subsurface hydrothermal plumbing.

These barite masses occur at the uppermost tips of hydrothermal feeder veins along faults (that is, hydrothermal fluid conduits), and some are found immediately beneath overlying strata with known geyserite and siliceous sinter deposits.

Therefore, regardless of whether the Dresser bubbles were derived from degassing of thermal fluids or represent metabolic gas derivatives, preservation likely occurred almost immediately, through entrapment in microbial EPS.

decisions.rationale: Retained 2017 Dresser results explicitly report three DFc1 localities about 2 km apart with microlaminated siliceous rocks interpreted as geyserite. The label and statement preserve attribution and geological setting. Claim kind, earth domain, site scope and placement as an independent node are justified; reported, undated and frontier=false carry only their neutral policy meanings. No edge or directional dependency is asserted.
decisions.limitations: Geological identification is the authors' inference; the captured source alone does not establish independent replication, biological origin or current consensus.

decisions.rationale: The authors explicitly interpret microlaminated rocks at three DFc1 localities approximately 2 km apart as geyserite. Exact quotations and offsets match. Claim kind, earth domain, neutral reported status, undated era and frontier=false are justified. No identity, taxonomy or directional relationship is proposed.
decisions.limitations: The interpretation relies on stratigraphic, petrographic and geochemical evidence and comparison with younger geyserite. It does not independently prove biological origin. The source notes a published correction whose effects were not separately assessed.

decisions.rationale: At locality 1S the paper describes a 3 cm siliceous unit above stratiform geyserite, with approximately 1 cm convex ridges less than 2 cm high, and says they resemble mid- to distal-apron sinter terracettes. The label, conditional interpretation, earth-domain claim classification, site placement and neutral metadata are faithful. No graph relation is introduced.
decisions.limitations: Resemblance to modern sinters is interpretive; the ridges' construction by microbes is not demonstrated by this specific finding.

decisions.rationale: Both retained excerpts exactly support the locality 1S ridge measurements and their interpretation as resembling mid- to distal-apron sinter terracettes. Scope and uncertainty are preserved. Claim/earth and neutral reported, undated and frontier=false metadata are appropriate. No relationship or identity merge is proposed.
decisions.limitations: Morphological resemblance and primary porosity support the proposed interpretation but do not establish direct microbial construction.

decisions.rationale: The paper explicitly proposes that at least some barite masses at upper hydrothermal vein tips are mineralized remnants of terrestrial hot-spring pools with shallow plumbing. The quantifier 'at least some' and proposed status are preserved. Claim identity, earth domain, local geological scope, standalone placement and neutral metadata are supported; no edge direction is claimed.
decisions.limitations: Subsurface-pool reconstruction is proposed from geological geometry; the paper does not extend it to every Dresser barite mass.

decisions.rationale: The retained source expressly proposes that at least some large barite masses represent mineralized terrestrial hot-spring pools and shallow hydrothermal plumbing. The candidate preserves that restriction and geological setting. Kind, domain and neutral metadata are justified without inventing relationships or identities.
decisions.limitations: This is an interpretive reassessment of selected barite masses. It does not establish that all Dresser barite masses formed as hot-spring pools.

decisions.rationale: The source describes numerous approximately 200 µm circular/subcircular structures at locality 16N, interprets them as bubbles, and says entrapment in microbial EPS likely preserved them regardless of thermal-fluid versus metabolic gas source. The statement, claim label, earth domain, site identity and neutral metadata keep these qualifications. No independent graph dependency is inserted.
decisions.limitations: Bubble identity and microbial-EPS trapping remain interpretations; the bubbles' actual gas provenance is unresolved.

decisions.rationale: Exact excerpts establish the approximately 200 µm circular structures and explicitly describe likely preservation in microbial EPS while leaving the source of the gas unresolved. The candidate attributes these interpretations rather than asserting demonstrated microbial gas production. Claim/earth and neutral representation metadata are justified; no relation, identity or placement beyond domain is proposed.
decisions.limitations: Bubble identification and EPS entrapment remain interpretations based on textures and analogues. Thermal-fluid degassing and metabolic gas production are both retained as possibilities.

decisions.rationale: The retained Dresser article reports vertically aligned, approximately 230 µm quartz crystals in some terracette laminae, suggesting analogy to recrystallized microbial palisade fabric from bedding-perpendicular silicified filaments. The candidate retains 'suggest' and 'analogous', with justified earth-domain claim identity, standalone placement and neutral metadata.
decisions.limitations: Quartz-fabric resemblance does not establish preserved cells, filament taxonomy or unique biogenicity.

decisions.rationale: The source describes 230 µm vertically aligned quartz crystals within the sinter-terracette unit and explicitly suggests analogy with recrystallized microbial palisade fabric. The candidate preserves the suggested rather than established classification. Claim/earth, reported, undated and frontier=false are justified. No unverified identity or relation appears.
decisions.limitations: The original biological filaments are inferred from mineral textures and geological context. Recrystallization prevents direct identification from this evidence alone.

decisions.rationale: The source places inferred geyserite rip-up clasts interbedded with domical and conical stromatolitic laminates at locality 24S and says tuffaceous sediment onlap plus internal microfabrics are consistent with microbial origin. The candidate retains the locality and nonexclusive interpretation. Claim kind, earth domain, site placement and neutral metadata are justified, with no graph direction asserted.
decisions.limitations: Consistency with microbial origin is not proof of exclusive microbial genesis; the geyserite-clast identification is itself interpretive.

decisions.rationale: The retained excerpts identify geyserite rip-up clasts interbedded with domical and conical stromatolitic laminates at locality 24S and describe their internal textures and sediment onlap as consistent with microbial origin. The statement retains this evidentiary limitation. Claim/earth and neutral metadata are appropriate; no unsupported relationship, identity or taxonomy is added.
decisions.limitations: Textures consistent with microbial activity do not uniquely establish biological origin. The finding is localized and cannot automatically classify other Dresser structures.

decisions.rationale: The 2018 paper describes a sampled suite of spheroidal-to-lenticular Dresser structures resembling some previously described Archean microfossils; correlative microscopy of size, walls and chemistry supports the authors' interpretation as silicified and pyritized vesicular volcanic glass. The claim is correctly limited to this suite, placed in earth science, and source-attributed with neutral metadata.
decisions.limitations: The study's abiogenic assessment applies only to the examined microstructures; it does not overturn all Dresser or Archean microfossil reports.

decisions.rationale: The retained primary source describes the studied spheroidal-to-lenticular microstructure suite and interprets it as silicified and pyritized vesicular volcanic glass using size distribution, wall ultrastructure and chemistry. The candidate accurately attributes this interpretation to the study. Kind, domain and neutral representation metadata are justified without identifying unrelated fossils as the same objects.
decisions.limitations: The abiogenic interpretation concerns the examined Dresser sample suite. It neither disproves every reported Archean microfossil nor automatically invalidates separate Dresser biosignatures.

decisions.rationale: The 2018 Dresser source explicitly reports kerogenous material associated with much altered volcanic glass, carbon lining/filling some vesicles, and organic-rich laminae enclosing multiple vesicles. These are associations, represented as such. The claim label, earth-domain scope, sampled-material identity and standalone placement match the retained article and neutral policy.
decisions.limitations: Associated kerogenous carbon does not by itself establish whether vesicles, laminae or carbon are biological.

decisions.rationale: The exact excerpt reports kerogenous material associated with altered volcanic glass, organic carbon lining or filling some vesicles, and organic-rich laminae surrounding multiple vesicles. The candidate preserves the observed association and its limited population. Claim/earth and neutral metadata are justified; no additional identity or classification is proposed.
decisions.limitations: Organic carbon accompanying volcanic structures does not demonstrate that the structures themselves are biological or establish the origin of the associated carbon.

decisions.rationale: The article warns that reworked, isolated silicified microstructures of the studied volcanic-glass type can adsorb carbon and become pyritized, confusing life-detection interpretation; in those cases nanoscale wall analysis is required to exclude a biological origin. The candidate weakens 'required' to 'may be required' but does not strengthen it; its scope is explicitly conditional. Earth-domain claim and neutral metadata fit.
decisions.limitations: Methodological warning is conditional for these volcanic-glass-like isolated structures, not a universal nanoscale requirement for every candidate biosignature.

decisions.rationale: The source explicitly warns that reworked isolated silicified structures of the studied type can adsorb carbon and become pyritized, creating difficulties in microfossil identification. It also identifies nanoscale wall analysis as a possible necessary discriminator. The candidate preserves the conditional warning. Claim/earth and neutral representation metadata are justified.
decisions.limitations: The caution concerns microstructures of this type. It cannot be generalized into a finding that all carbon-coated Archean or extraterrestrial fossil candidates are abiotic.

decisions.rationale: The 2018 controlled batch-incubation paper reports B. fungorum growth on HSDP2 basalt and Fe/major-element release exceeding abiotic controls only in nutrient-depleted rock-sample assays. The statement keeps the organism, rock source, comparison and exclusivity limited to these assays. The earth-domain claim, neutral metadata and independent-node placement are justified.
decisions.limitations: Limited to a single bacterium and specified laboratory nutrient conditions; no general field-scale or oceanic release rate is established.

decisions.rationale: The retained study explicitly states that Fe and other major-element release from HSDP2 drill-core basalt exceeded abiotic controls only when the rock-sample assay was nutrient depleted. The candidate retains the single-species laboratory context and limiting condition. Claim/earth, reported, undated and frontier=false are appropriate, with no asserted relationship or identity merge.
decisions.limitations: The experiments used Burkholderia fungorum under controlled laboratory conditions with added glucose and low-salt medium. The result does not establish the same response across natural microbial communities, seawater or all basalt environments.

decisions.rationale: The retained 2018 source directly says dissolved major-element concentrations in biotic synthetic-basalt-glass colonization experiments increased with increasing residual stress and Fe(II) content. The candidate represents an association over the tested glasses, not separately isolated causation. Claim classification, earth domain, lab scope, descriptive comparison direction and neutral metadata are faithful.
decisions.limitations: Residual stress and Fe(II) vary across the reported treatments, so individual independent causal contributions cannot be inferred.

decisions.rationale: The retained source explicitly reports that dissolved major-element concentrations in biotic synthetic-basalt-glass colonization assays increased with residual stress and Fe(II) content. The candidate treats the finding as a reported laboratory association and preserves its joint-factor limitation. Claim/earth and neutral metadata are justified without additional placement or relations.
decisions.limitations: Residual stress and Fe(II) content are not established here as individually isolated causal mechanisms. The finding does not support a universal microbial dissolution rate or response across all basalt glasses.

decisions.rationale: The source directly contrasts intensely biofilm-covered synthetic basalt glasses with residual stress and high Fe(II) against sparse colonization on unstressed, high-Fe(III) glasses. The statement and label retain both coupled conditions and comparison direction. Earth-domain claim, laboratory scope, independent placement and neutral metadata are justified.
decisions.limitations: Stress and iron oxidation state change together in this comparison; neither is proved the sole driver of biofilm coverage.

decisions.rationale: The retained excerpt directly contrasts intense cellular biofilm coverage on stressed Fe(II)-rich basaltic glasses with sparse colonization on unstressed Fe(III)-rich glasses. Dense versus sparse accurately preserves that comparison. Kind, earth domain, reported status, undated era and frontier=false are justified. No unsupported relationship or identity merge is proposed.
decisions.limitations: The contrasted glasses differ jointly in oxidation state and residual stress, so the result cannot isolate either factor as the sole cause. The conclusion is restricted to the reported laboratory colonization assays.

The cause of the Cit
−
lineage’s extinction remains unknown. We have rejected our initial hypothesis that on-going adaptation of the Cit
+

−

The candidate preserves the three starting conditions, replicate counts, propagation durations and observed outcome. Claim kind, life domain, standalone identity and neutral metadata are justified.
decisions.limitations: The one extended replay is separate from the 40 shorter replays. Failure to reproduce extinction under standard conditions does not prove competitive extinction impossible or reproduce an unidentified historical laboratory perturbation. The candidate does not establish a universal survival guarantee.

decisions.rationale: Turner explicitly reports that a 43,000-generation Cit− clone invaded the 50,000-generation Ara−3 resident population and reached roughly 3 × 10^5 cells/mL, about tenfold below other treatments. The candidate preserves generation direction, measurement unit and the mean across high- and low-density starts. Kind, domain and neutral metadata are suitable.
decisions.limitations: The assay spans seven days, and invasion under these conditions does not show indefinite stable coexistence or resolve the earlier extinction.

decisions.rationale: The Turner source explicitly states that a generation-43,000 Cit− clone invaded a resident generation-50,000 population and reports a final mean Cit− density of approximately 3 × 10^5 cells/mL, about an order of magnitude below densities in the other treatments. The candidate preserves which population supplied the invading clone, which was the recipient, and the quantitative result. Life-domain claim identity, neutral metadata and independent representation are justified.
decisions.limitations: The measured density is the mean across high- and low-inoculum treatments in a short competition experiment. Successful reinvasion does not establish indefinite stable coexistence, an invariant ecological equilibrium or the cause of the original Cit− loss. The source does not justify reversing the invasion direction.

decisions.rationale: Turner explicitly states that the Cit− extinction cause remains unknown, rejects the authors' initial ongoing Cit+ adaptation explanation, and offers an unidentified rare random catastrophe as a proposed explanation. The node attributes the hypothesis, does not assert an observed catastrophe, and preserves the scoped historical uncertainty, life domain, kind and neutral metadata.
decisions.limitations: Proposed events such as residue or water issues were not observed. The evidence does not eliminate every possible ecological or fitness-related extinction mechanism.

decisions.rationale: Turner et al. explicitly state that the cause of Ara−3 Cit− lineage extinction remains unknown. They reject their initial ongoing-Cit+ adaptation explanation and propose a rare random catastrophe as a possible account, while acknowledging that its nature is unknown. The candidate clearly marks the perturbation as proposed rather than observed. The claim kind, life domain, historical attribution, neutral status, unresolved era, frontier=false and independent identity are justified.
decisions.limitations: The source does not demonstrate that a random catastrophe occurred, establish a particular laboratory error, or eliminate every conceivable fitness-mediated or ecological explanation. support.quote: We analyze the performance of language models on two tasks that require identifying relevant information in their input contexts: multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval.

In particular, we observe that performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context, and significantly degrades when models must access relevant information in the middle of long contexts, even for explicitly long-context models.

canonical_record.label: JUNO 207-day atmospheric mass-splitting fits
canonical_record.summary: The September 2026 JUNO analysis reported 8,294 inverse-beta-decay candidates in 207.2 live days at an average 52.5 km reactor baseline and obtained different fitted atmospheric mass splittings under normal and inverted ordering using a Daya Bay constraint.

support.quote: The analysis is based on 207.2 live days of data, comprising 8,294 inverse beta-decay candidates collected at an average reactor baseline of 52.5 km. A world-leading precision of approximately 1% was achieved for the atmospheric neutrino mass splitting $\Delta m^2_{31}$, with $\Delta m^2_{31}=+2.509^{+0.027}_{-0.025}\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{eV}^2$ for normal ordering and $\Delta m^2_{31}=-2.482^{+0.025}_{-0.026}\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{eV}^2$ for inverted ordering, using the Daya Bay constraint in the fit to resolve the correct physical minimum under each mass-ordering hypothesis.

canonical_record.label: Kurvers spatial producer-scrounger evolutionary simulation
canonical_record.summary: Kurvers and colleagues modeled group foraging with a spatially explicit genetic algorithm whose simulated agents could alternate between producing and scrounging; the exploration level and the probability of scrounging were distinct, evolving continuous traits each ranging from 0 to 1.

assertions.statement: Kurvers and colleagues modeled group foraging with a spatially explicit genetic algorithm whose simulated agents could alternate between producing and scrounging; the exploration level and the probability of scrounging were distinct, evolving continuous traits each ranging from 0 to 1.

scope.population: Simulated agents in a spatial producer-scrounger foraging game
scope.time: 2012 publication; tactics alternated within foraging rounds and genetic traits evolved across rounds
scope.assumptions: Exploration is a level or score affecting spatial movement and social attraction, not itself defined as the probability of exploring; scrounging probability governs tactic selection.
scope.uncertainty: Computational model rather than direct animal observation; outcomes depend on implemented spatial and selection assumptions.
scope.units: Dimensionless exploration level and scrounging probability, each on [0,1]
scope.quantifiers: Both traits continuous and evolvable; no fixed producer/scrounger or fast/slow types were imposed initially.

support.quote:
Here we incorporated travel times for scroungers and allowed individuals to play a mixed strategy by alternating between producer and scrounger within rounds. Importantly, we did not start with

Both the level of exploration and the scrounging probability were on a continuous scale (0–1) and were allowed to evolve (i.e., not fixed).

canonical_record.label: Ba-La-Cu-O: tentative 30 K onset (1986)
canonical_record.summary: Bednorz and Mueller reported an abrupt resistivity decrease of up to three orders of magnitude in multiphase, oxygen-deficient polycrystalline Ba-La-Cu-O samples, with the highest onset in the 30 K range and suppression at high current density; they described this as reminiscent of percolative superconductivity.

assertions.statement: Bednorz and Mueller reported an abrupt resistivity decrease of up to three orders of magnitude in multiphase, oxygen-deficient polycrystalline Ba-La-Cu-O samples, with the highest onset in the 30 K range and suppression at high current density; they described this as reminiscent of percolative superconductivity.

scope.population: Multiphase oxygen-deficient polycrystalline Ba-La-Cu-O; x=1 or 0.75, y>0
assumptions: Annealing below 900 degrees C under reducing conditions
scope.uncertainty: Tentative resistive interpretation in the original abstract; no claim here of bulk Meissner confirmation.
scope.quantifiers: Only the cited samples, apparatus, or proposal; no universal extension.

support.quote: Metallic, oxygen-deficient compounds in the Ba-La-Cu-O system, with the composition BaxLa5-xCu5O5(3-y) have been prepared in polycrystalline form. Samples with x=1 and 0.75, y>0, annealed below 900°C under reducing conditions, consist of three phases, one of them a perovskite-like mixed-valent copper compound. Upon cooling, the samples show a linear decrease in resistivity, then an approximately logarithmic increase, interpreted as a beginning of localization. Finally an abrupt decrease by up to three orders of magnitude occurs, reminiscent of the onset of percolative superconductivity. The highest onset temperature is observed in the 30 K range. It is markedly reduced by high current densities. Thus, it results partially from the percolative nature, bute possibly also from 2 D superconducting fluctuations of double perovskite layers of one of the phases present. © 1986 Springer-Verlag.

Superconductivity at 93 K in a new mixed-phase Y-Ba-Cu-O compound system at ambient pressure
A stable and reproducible superconductivity transition between 80 and 93 K has been achieved and maintained in a Y-Ba-Cu-O compound system at ambient pressure in a simple liquid-nitrogen Dewar. An upper critical field Hc2(0) estimate of between 80 and 180 T is obtained, and the paramagnetic limiting field at 0 K for a sample with a T(c) of about 90 K is 165 T. It is suggested that the lattice parameters, the valence ratio, and the sample treatments all play a role in achieving superconductivity above 77 K.

canonical_record.label: YBCO grain-boundary orientation limits (1988)
canonical_record.summary: Dimos et al. measured grain-boundary critical current densities as a function of basal-plane misorientation in YBCO bicrystals and concluded that strong texture both normal to and within the basal plane is important for very high critical currents in pure polycrystalline samples.

assertions.statement: Dimos et al. measured grain-boundary critical current densities as a function of basal-plane misorientation in YBCO bicrystals and concluded that strong texture both normal to and within the basal plane is important for very high critical currents in pure polycrystalline samples.

scope.population: YBCO bicrystals; implication scoped to pure polycrystalline samples
assumptions: Basal-plane grain misorientation is the varied parameter
scope.uncertainty: Author-institution abstract only; its incomplete chemical formula and malformed large-angle numerical ratio are not repaired or interpreted.
scope.quantifiers: Only the cited samples, apparatus, or proposal; no universal extension.

support.quote: The critical current densities across grain boundaries have been measured as a function of misorientation angle in the basal plane of bicrystals of YBa2Cu3O7-. For small misorientation angles, the ratio of the grain-boundary critical current density to the bulk critical current density is roughly proportional to the inverse of the misorientation angle; for large angles, this ratio saturates to a value of about 150. These results imply that achieving a high degree of texture both normal to and within the basal plane is important for the obtaining of very high critical currents in pure polycrystalline samples. © 1988 The American Physical Society.

canonical_record.label: Biaxially textured metal substrates for YBCO tapes (1996)
canonical_record.summary: Goyal et al. reported a route using industrially scalable thermomechanical texturing of flexible metal substrates followed by epitaxial buffer layers and YBa2Cu3Ox films; the deposited films carried critical currents at 77 K in zero field and had field dependencies similar to epitaxial films on single-crystal ceramic substrates.
