context_nodes.label: string matching with errors
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines string matching with errors as: Searching for approximate (e.g., up to a predefined number of symbol mismatches, insertions, and deletions) occurrences of a pattern string in a text string. Preprocessing, e.g., building an index, may or may not be allowed. Also known as approximate string matching.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stringMatchwError

context_nodes.label: strip packing
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strip packing as: Pack a set of rectangles into a strip of width 1 to minimize the height used. Rectangles may not overlap or be rotated. Without loss of generality, the height of rectangles is at most 1. This is NP-hard .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strippacking

context_nodes.label: strongly connected component
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strongly connected component as: A strongly connected subgraph , S, of a directed graph , D, such that no vertex of D can be added to S and it still be strongly connected. Informally, a maximal subgraph in which every vertex is reachable from every other vertex.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stronglyConnectedCompo

context_nodes.label: strongly connected graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strongly connected graph as: A directed graph that has a path from each vertex to every other vertex. Formal Definition: A directed graph D=(V, E) such that for all pairs of vertices u, v ∈ V, there is a path from u to v and from v to u.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stronglyConnectedGraph

context_nodes.label: strongly NP-hard
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strongly NP-hard as: The complexity class of decision problems which are still NP-hard even when all numbers in the input are bounded by some polynomial in the length of the input.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stronglyNP

context_nodes.label: sublinear time algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sublinear time algorithm as: A algorithm whose execution time, f(n), grows slower than the size of the problem, n, but only gives an approximate or probably correct answer.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sublinearTimeAlgo

context_nodes.label: subset
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines subset as: A set S 1 is a subset of another set S 2 if every element in S 1 is in S 2 . S 2 may have exactly the same elements as S 1 . Formal Definition: S 1 ⊆ S 2 iff ∀ s, s ∈ S 1 → s ∈ S 2 .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: subset

context_nodes.label: tail recursion
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines tail recursion as: A special form of recursion where the last operation of a function is a recursive call. The recursion may be optimized away by executing the call in the current stack frame and returning its result rather than creating a new stack frame.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: tailRecursion

context_nodes.label: total function
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines total function as: A function which is defined for all inputs of the right type, that is, for all of a domain .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: totalfunc

context_nodes.label: traveling salesman
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines traveling salesman as: Find a path through a weighted graph that starts and ends at the same vertex , includes every other vertex exactly once, and minimizes the total cost of edges . Also known as TSP.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: travelingSalesman

context_nodes.label: trinary function
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines trinary function as: A function with three arguments.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: trinaryfunc

context_nodes.label: unary function
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines unary function as: A function which takes one argument.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: unaryfunc

context_nodes.label: undecidable problem
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines undecidable problem as: A problem that cannot be solved for all cases by any algorithm whatsoever---equivalently, whose associated language cannot be recognized by a Turing machine that halts for all inputs.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: undecidableProblem

context_nodes.label: undirected graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines undirected graph as: A graph whose edges are unordered pairs of vertices . That is, each edge connects two vertices. Formal Definition: A graph G is a pair (V,E), where V is a set of vertices, and E is a set of edges between the vertices E ⊆ {{u,v} | u, v ∈ V}. If the graph does not allow self-loops , adjacency is irreflexive , that is E ⊆ {{u,v} | u, v ∈ V ∧ u ≠ v}.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: undirectedGraph

context_nodes.label: universal Turing machine
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines universal Turing machine as: A Turing machine that is capable of simulating any other Turing machine by encoding the latter.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: universalTur

context_nodes.label: vehicle routing problem
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines vehicle routing problem as: Find an optimal route of one or more vehicles through a graph . Also known as VRP.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: vehicleRouting

context_nodes.label: weighted, directed graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines weighted, directed graph as: A directed graph that has a weight, or numeric value, associated with each edge .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: weightedDigraph

context_nodes.label: Medicine
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Medicine as: The art and science of studying, performing research on, preventing, diagnosing, and treating disease, as well as the maintenance of health.

context_nodes.label: Internal Medicine
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Internal Medicine as: A medical specialty concerned with the diagnosis and treatment of diseases of the internal organ systems of adults.

context_nodes.label: Pediatrics
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Pediatrics as: A medical specialty concerned with maintaining health and providing medical care to children from birth to adolescence.

context_nodes.label: Reproductive Medicine
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Reproductive Medicine as: A medical-surgical specialty concerned with the morphology, physiology, biochemistry, and pathology of reproduction in man and other animals, and on the biological, medical, and veterinary problems of fertility and lactation. It includes ovulation induction, diagnosis of infertility and recurrent pregnancy loss, and assisted reproductive technologies such as embryo transfer, in vitro fertilization, and intrafallopian transfer of zygotes. (From Infertility and Reproductive Medicine Clinics of North America, Foreword 1990; Journal of Reproduction and Fertility, Notice to Contributors, Jan 1979)

context_nodes.label: Specialties, Surgical
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Specialties, Surgical as: Various branches of surgical practice limited to specialized areas.

context_nodes.label: Acute Care Surgery
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Acute Care Surgery as: Surgical specialty generally encompassing emergency general surgery, surgical critical care and trauma care. Acute care surgery is a component of general surgery related to care of patients with acute, life-threatening or potentially life-threatening surgical conditions.

context_nodes.label: Humanities
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Humanities as: Fields of inquiry in human constructs and concerns as opposed to natural processes and social relations. These are traditionally the study of literature, philosophy, and religion.

context_nodes.label: Ethical Dilemmas
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Ethical Dilemmas as: Situations in which two moral principles conflict with one another. Fictional or hypothetical dilemmas of this kind are used to assess the moral beliefs or moral reasoning skills of individuals. (From APA Dictionary of Psychology, https://dictionary.apa.org/)

context_nodes.label: Fuzzy Logic
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Fuzzy Logic as: Approximate, quantitative reasoning that is concerned with the linguistic ambiguity which exists in natural or synthetic language. At its core are variables such as good, bad, and young as well as modifiers such as more, less, and very. These ordinary terms represent fuzzy sets in a particular problem. Fuzzy logic plays a key role in many medical expert systems.

context_nodes.label: Ethics
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Ethics as: The philosophy or code pertaining to what is ideal in human character and conduct. Also, the field of study dealing with the principles of morality.

context_nodes.label: Social Sciences
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Social Sciences as: Disciplines concerned with the interrelationships of individuals in a social environment including social organizations and institutions. Includes Sociology and Anthropology.

context_nodes.label: Environment Design
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Environment Design as: The structuring of the environment to permit or promote specific patterns of behavior.

context_nodes.label: Government
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Government as: The complex of political institutions, laws, and customs through which the function of governing is carried out in a specific political unit.

context_nodes.label: Federal Government
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Federal Government as: The level of governmental organization and function at the national or country-wide level.

context_nodes.label: Nervous System Diseases
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Nervous System Diseases as: Diseases of the central and peripheral nervous system. This includes disorders of the brain, spinal cord, cranial nerves, peripheral nerves, nerve roots, autonomic nervous system, neuromuscular junction, and muscle.

context_nodes.label: Communicable Diseases
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Communicable Diseases as: An illness caused by an infectious agent or its toxins that occurs through the direct or indirect transmission of the infectious agent or its products from an infected individual or via an animal, vector or the inanimate environment to a susceptible animal or human host.

context_nodes.label: Sexually Transmitted Diseases
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Sexually Transmitted Diseases as: Diseases due to or propagated by sexual contact.

context_nodes.label: Restless Legs Syndrome
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Restless Legs Syndrome as: A disorder characterized by aching or burning sensations in the lower and rarely the upper extremities that occur prior to sleep or may awaken the patient from sleep.

context_nodes.label: Behavior and Behavior Mechanisms
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Behavior and Behavior Mechanisms as: The observable response made to a situation and the unconscious processes underlying it.

context_nodes.label: Behavior
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Behavior as: The observable response of a man or animal to a situation.

context_nodes.label: Motivation
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Motivation as: Those factors which cause an organism to behave or act in either a goal-seeking or satisfying manner. They may be influenced by physiological drives or by external stimuli.

context_nodes.label: Behavior, Animal
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Behavior, Animal as: The observable response an animal makes to any situation.

context_nodes.label: Communication
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Communication as: The exchange or transmission of ideas, attitudes, or beliefs between individuals or groups.

context_nodes.label: Escape Reaction
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Escape Reaction as: Innate response elicited by sensory stimuli associated with a threatening situation, or actual confrontation with an enemy.

context_nodes.label: Feeding Behavior
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Feeding Behavior as: Behavioral responses or sequences associated with eating including modes of feeding, rhythmic patterns of eating, and time intervals.

context_nodes.label: Information Seeking Behavior
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Information Seeking Behavior as: How information is gathered in personal, academic or work environments and the resources used.

context_nodes.label: Codes of Ethics
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Codes of Ethics as: Systematic statements of principles or rules of appropriate professional conduct, usually established by professional societies.

context_nodes.label: Engineering
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Engineering as: The practical application of physical, mechanical, and mathematical principles. (Stedman, 25th ed)

context_nodes.label: User-Centered Design
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes User-Centered Design as: Design process using input from users regarding systems, devices, or software.

context_nodes.label: Mathematics
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Mathematics as: The deductive study of shape, quantity, and dependence. (From McGraw-Hill Dictionary of Scientific and Technical Terms, 6th ed)

context_nodes.label: Risk
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Risk as: The probability that an event will occur. It encompasses a variety of measures of the probability of a generally unfavorable outcome.

context_nodes.label: Correlation of Data
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Correlation of Data as: Determination of whether or not two variables are correlated. This means to study whether an increase or decrease in one variable corresponds to an increase or decrease in the other variable.

context_nodes.label: Adverse Outcome Pathways
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Adverse Outcome Pathways as: Models connecting initiating events at the cellular and molecular level to population-wide impacts. Computational models may be at levels relating toxicology to adverse effects.

context_nodes.label: Healthcare Failure Mode and Effect Analysis
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Healthcare Failure Mode and Effect Analysis as: Prospective risk assessment tool aimed at identifying potential risks and their impact in healthcare settings.

context_nodes.label: Genetic Risk Score
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Genetic Risk Score as: Estimate of an individual's genetic liability to a trait or disease, calculated according to their genotype profile and relevant genome-wide association study data. (from Tutorial: a guide to performing polygenic risk score analyses. Nat Protoc. 2020 Sep;15(9):2759.)

context_nodes.label: Heart Disease Risk Factors
context_nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Heart Disease Risk Factors as: Aspects of personal behavior or lifestyle, environmental exposure, inherited conditions and characteristics, which are determined to be associated with HEART DISEASES .

context_nodes.label: immune system process
context_nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines immune system process as: Any process involved in the development or functioning of the immune system, an organismal system for calibrated responses to potential internal or invasive threats.

context_nodes.label: immune response
context_nodes.summary: The Gene Ontology (via EMBL-EBI QuickGO) defines immune response as: Any immune system process that functions in the calibrated response of an organism to a potential internal or invasive threat.

context_nodes.label: religious concepts
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religious concepts as: Ideas and notions that are fundamentally religious.

context_nodes.label: philosophical concepts
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines philosophical concepts as: Concepts related to knowledge, learning, and scholarship.

context_nodes.label: book history
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines book history as: Research into the evolution of the book and its variants (pamphlets, newspapers, broadsheets) in all aspects of its production, dissemination and consumption in relation to literary, political, economical, social and religious history. The history of the book includes subjects such as the production of manuscripts in medieval scriptoria, authorship, printing techniques, economic aspects of printing and publishing, design, printshops and publishing houses, trade, ownership and reading culture, typography, typesetting and printing techniques, and book collecting and connoisseurship. Use " literary history" Use “literary history” for the study of literary trends and movements.

context_nodes.label: literary studies
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines literary studies as: Discipline dealing with the written and oral verbal works of a nation, region, period, or language, of a particular group or individual, of a particular form or genre, on a particular subject, or for a particular audience. For written works on a particular subject, use "literature (documents)." For the written works of a particular individual or group of individuals, use "writings (documents)." For the genre of liturature rather than the discipline that studies it, use "literature (genre)." Use "book history" for the study of the trade, production, and consumption of books as physical objects.

context_nodes.label: museology
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines museology as: The theory and practice of the organization, administration, functions, and technical processes of museums, including documentation and collections management, as well as their history, philosophy, and purposes.

context_nodes.label: paper history
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines paper history as: Study of the origin and evolution of paper as a product and material: paper production, paper trade, the management of papermills and paper factories, raw materials, and the cultural importance of paper as an information carrier.

context_nodes.label: religious ideologies
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religious ideologies as: Organized bodies of ideas and attitudes having to do with religion, which is broadly defined as belief systems that encompass various personal and institutional relationships between human beings and what they regard as holy, sacred, or divine, usually but not always a deity, or a spiritual or occult force.

context_nodes.label: aesthetic concepts
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines aesthetic concepts as: Concepts related to perception of what is ideal or beautiful.

context_nodes.label: theater arts
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines theater arts as: Broad discipline concerning drama, dance, critical studies, and theater design/technology; a professionally-oriented study of theater, that involves training, practice, and study in the processes of doing theater.

context_nodes.label: electronic music
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines electronic music as: Music in which sound is generated, transferred, triggered, or amplified by electronic devices. The creation of electronic music may involve the use of magnetic tape or digital technology and whose reproduction involves the use of loudspeakers. For works created with only natural sound sources recorded and manipulated via discs or magnetic tape use "musique concrète." For music created entirely through the use of a computer, in which the sound is initiated purely through digital means, use "computer music."

context_nodes.label: jazz
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines jazz as: Music, often improvisational, originally developed around the turn of the 20th century by African Americans from elements of blues and ragtime, with syncopated rhythms and a European harmonic structure. Jazz consistently evolved throughout the 20th century with numerous phases, from a New Orleans style or swing, to "free jazz," for example, which emerged in the late 1950s. Therefore, jazz itself has no precise definition, however it has rarely been a completely composed music.

context_nodes.label: musical theater
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines musical theater as: Genre of theatrical performance that combines songs, spoken dialogue, acting, and dance.

context_nodes.label: rhythm and blues
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines rhythm and blues as: Any of various kinds of popular music typically having a strong rhythm and featuring a horn section. Originally and principally associated with African-American performers, particularly a style prominent during the late 1940s and 1950s derived from or influenced by the blues and jazz.

context_nodes.label: serial music
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines serial music as: A structural principle for musical composition used since the early 20th century in which a series or set of elements are used repeatedly.

context_nodes.label: arts-related disciplines
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines arts-related disciplines as: Branches of learning devoted to the arts.

context_nodes.label: linguistics
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines linguistics as: Scientific study of language as a system, covering the structure, sounds, and meaning, as well as the history of the relations of languages to each other and the cultural place of language in human behavior.

context_nodes.label: linguistics-related disciplines
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines linguistics-related disciplines as: Branches of learning and professions related to linguistics.

context_nodes.label: aesthetics
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines aesthetics as: Appreciation or criticism of the beautiful. The term refers to a branch of Western philosophy concerned primarily with the fine arts, although it may also be used in the context of the appreciation of natural beauty. Usage of the term dates from the 18th century, although historical discussions regarding issues now called "aesthetics" date from Antiquity.

context_nodes.label: axiology
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines axiology as: Study of values, primarily of intrinsic values (as those in ethics, aesthetics, and religion), but also of instrumental values (as those in economics), particularly with reference to the manner in which they can be known or experienced, their nature and kinds, and their ontological status.

context_nodes.label: phenomenology
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines phenomenology as: Branch of modern philosophy dealing with the description and classification of phenomena.

context_nodes.label: philosophy of art
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines philosophy of art as: The study of the nature of art, including interpretation, representation, expression, and form. It is closely related to "aesthetics," which is the philosophical study of beauty.

context_nodes.label: teleology
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines teleology as: Philosophical study of finality, especially as it pertains to design or purposes in the processes of nature.

context_nodes.label: religion-related disciplines
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines religion-related disciplines as: Branches of learning devoted to religion.

context_nodes.label: social ethics
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines social ethics as: Ethics that have as their utilitarian end the well-being and fair treatment of the entire community.

context_nodes.label: Augustinianism
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Augustinianism as: Refers to the philosophical and theological ideas and doctrines derived from the work of Augustine (354-430), bishop of Hippo, and associated with the Augustinian orders. The intellectual tradition of Augustinianism has been influential since the Middle Ages, when it developed. Augustine offered an optimistic ontology and an escape from skepticism. He also formulated a cosmic theory to account for the plurality of form in the world and to reconcile it with the uniqueness of God's creative act. Augustine also described the ultimate goal of human life as a life of beatitude combined with ethical-political concern. Primacy of faith, knowledge of the soul, divine illumination, and grace are all essential aspects of Augustinianism. Augustine believed that truth resided in man's soul and it was this truth alone that instructs man. This truth, the greatest proof of God's existence, confers joy and happiness. Augustine's speculation on the Trinity and predestination were also highly influential.

context_nodes.label: determinism
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines determinism as: Doctrine that all acts of will result from causes which determine them either in such a manner that people have no alternative course of action, or that the will is still free in the sense of being uncompelled. Determinism holds that all behaviors and events are determined by God or by the laws of the universe before they occur. Determinism takes different forms in religions, but the basic issue is how to reconcile the omnipotence of God or the inevitable effects of karma with the freedom and resposibility of a individual person.

context_nodes.label: choreography
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines choreography as: The aspect of the discipline of dance that involves inventing or arranging and putting together steps, gestures, and patterns to form dances, and separate dances to form a dance composition.

context_nodes.label: music theory
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines music theory as: Discipline involving the study of the theoretical aspects of music and its notation, typically as opposed to actual performance.

context_nodes.label: vocal arts
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines vocal arts as: Discipline involving the study of singing and other vocal expressions, including performance.

context_nodes.label: theoretical linguistics
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines theoretical linguistics as: Branch of linguistics where the primary aim is to establish universal principles for the study of language and languages, and to determine the underlying structure and other characteristics of human language.

context_nodes.label: process philosophy
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines process philosophy as: Refers to the theistic philosophy that views creative becoming as the universal form of reality and emphasizes the relational nature of all being.

context_nodes.label: anthropology of religion
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines anthropology of religion as: Study of religion using the methods and theories of anthropology.

context_nodes.label: comparative religion
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines comparative religion as: Comparative study of the characteristics of religious systems in different societies that focuses on the origin and evolution of religious beliefs and practices from earlier or less urbanized societies to modern ones, aims to develop a universal evolutionary continuum of religions, and stresses a scientific methodology. For the comparative study of religions that largely disregards evolutionary schemes and features a primarily historical methodology, use "religious history."

context_nodes.label: philosophy of religion
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines philosophy of religion as: The philosophical study of religion, especially concerning the rationality of religious beliefs, and the descriptive analysis and elucidation of religious language, belief, and practice.

context_nodes.label: psychology of religion
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines psychology of religion as: Branch of religious study in which religious thought, experience, and behavior are studied using the concepts and methodology of psychology.

context_nodes.label: sociology of religion
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines sociology of religion as: Study of religion using the sociological method of approach.

context_nodes.label: Asian
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Asian as: Refers to the cultures of the continent of Asia, which is in the eastern hemisphere, and is bounded by the Pacific Ocean, the Indian Ocean, the Arctic Ocean, and is generally considered to be delimited on the west by the Ural Mountains. It also refers to the numerous islands off the coast of Asia.

context_nodes.label: Middle Eastern
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Middle Eastern as: Styles and cultures existing in the extensive area that includes the nations of southwest Asia and northeastern Africa. The term was formerly used to also include Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, and Burma.

context_nodes.label: plastic arts
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines plastic arts as: In general, refers to the visual arts as opposed to literature, poetry, or other writing. In a narrower sense, it sometimes refers to all visual arts concerned with three-dimensional objects, but not two-dimensional visual arts. For works made of the material plastic, use "plastic (organic material)."

context_nodes.label: automotive design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines automotive design as: Practice and discipline of designing the appearance, ergonomics, complex systems, and other aspects of motor vehicles, usually road vehicles such as automobiles, motorcycles, trucks, buses, coaches, and vans.

context_nodes.label: communication design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines communication design as: Discipline that focuses on the presentation of information using visual and written elements. Communication design is a broad concept covering various disciplines, such as advertising, branding, web design, user interface design, information design, and social media. Communication designers focus on the strategy, content, and context of their messages, and how they can influence the behavior, attitude, and perception of their audience. Communication design uses research, analysis, storytelling, and user testing to create effective and engaging visual solutions that meet the needs and goals of clients and users.

context_nodes.label: costume design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines costume design as: Designing clothing, accessories, and ensembles intended to create an appearance characteristic of a particular period, person, place, or thing, especially (but not exclusively) for theatrical performances. For the design of clothing and accessories for personal wear, use "fashion design."

context_nodes.label: fashion design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines fashion design as: Designing clothing, accessories, and ensembles for personal wear. For the design of clothing, accessories, and ensembles intended to create an appearance characteristic of a particular period, person, place, or thing, especially (but not exclusively) for theatrical performances, use "costume design." For the concept of a prevailing, usually short lived custom, usage, or style in clothing, cars, restaurants, and other personal possessions and services, use "fashion."

context_nodes.label: furniture design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines furniture design as: Practice and discipline of designing furniture.

context_nodes.label: garden design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines garden design as: Discipline specializing in garden projects that are most often sited at a residence. Garden design is generally of smaller scale than landscape design, and may have defined boundaries.The practice differs from landscape architecture in the level of accreditation of the practitioner. For the discipline that requires licensed architects to design the use of outdoor space and the land, and that may include site planning, urban planning, park and recreation planning, garden design and historic preservation, use 'landscape architecture.'

context_nodes.label: graphic design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines graphic design as: The process of designing visual communications and text for commercial applications, usually to be printed or reproduced photographically, such as in advertisements, books, magazines, newspapers, leaflets, posters, diagrams, trademarks, corporate identities, sign systems, packaging, film, television graphics, etc.

context_nodes.label: industrial design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines industrial design as: The design of functional objects that can be mass-produced, including machine-made consumer and commercial products.

context_nodes.label: interior decoration
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines interior decoration as: The discipline focused on selecting and organizing the surface coverings, draperies, furniture, and furnishings of architectural interiors, usually of existing spaces.

context_nodes.label: interior design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines interior design as: Discipline specializing in the design of interiors of homes or other buildings, including placement of furniture, accessories, aesthetic or decorative schemes, and spatial arrangements, construction, building systems, acoustics, lighting, heating, and air conditioning of spaces. May refer to design for existing spaces or for spaces in the planning phases. For the discipline limited to the choices of color, texture, and superficial arrangement of furnishings of a space, prefer "interior decoration." For the discipline focusing more on the architecture of the interior, prefer "interior architecture (discipline)."

context_nodes.label: jewelry design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines jewelry design as: Discipline and activity of designing ornaments such as bracelets, necklaces, and rings for personal adornment.

context_nodes.label: paper engineering
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines paper engineering as: Design of paper structures and mechanisms, such as pop-up elements in books and greeting cards, cut-and-assemble paper models, and various types of paper containers.

context_nodes.label: participatory design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines participatory design as: Participation by workers and residents in the design of the spaces, structures, or communities which they use or inhabit.

context_nodes.label: set design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines set design as: The discipline and practice of designing and creating the sets, that is the physical surroundings in which the action takes place, for films, television, or theater.

context_nodes.label: textile design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines textile design as: Practice and discipline of designing textiles.

context_nodes.label: Web design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Web design as: Refers to the practice of designing for Websites, including graphical functional, and structural considerations.

context_nodes.label: architectural photography
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines architectural photography as: Specialization of photography focused on architecture as subject.

context_nodes.label: prehistoric African
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines prehistoric African as: Cultures and styles from the prehistoric era in Africa.

context_nodes.label: Ancient African
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Ancient African as: Cultures and styles of Africa in ancient times.

context_nodes.label: Colonial African
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Colonial African as: Styles and cultures belonging to Africa under colonial, usually European, rule or influence.

context_nodes.label: modern African
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines modern African as: Styles and cultures belonging to modern Africa, generally from the 19th century and later.

context_nodes.label: African sculpture styles
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines African sculpture styles as: Sculpture styles belonging to African cultures.

context_nodes.label: African diaspora
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines African diaspora as: Culture of the body of people who were displaced from their African homeland, and their descendants. Examples include those who traveled in ancient migrations and those who were involuntarily transported due to enslavement.

context_nodes.label: architectonics
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines architectonics as: The study of the scientific or technical aspects of architecture as distinguished from the purely artistic or historical aspect.

context_nodes.label: naval architecture
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines naval architecture as: Art or science of designing and building ships and other waterborne craft.

context_nodes.label: urban design
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines urban design as: The field of study and practice of designing the specific appearance, integration, and function of cities, towns, and villages. It is an interdisciplinary field that works with many built environment professions, including urban planning, architecture, landscape architecture, and civil engineering. For the field concerned with long-term planning for additions and improvements to the spatial organization and content of urban areas, use “urban planning.”

context_nodes.label: vāstuvidyā
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines vāstuvidyā as: In Indian architecture, a science of building, architecture.

context_nodes.label: syntax
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines syntax as: That branch of grammar that studies the formation of sentences, the relationships among their component words, clauses, and phrases, and the rules governing word order in a given language.

context_nodes.label: Libyan
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Libyan as: Style and culture of inhabitants of the large ancient country, Libya, in North Africa, or of the modern state of Libya.

context_nodes.label: Afanasievo
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Afanasievo as: Refers to the Neolithic culture established in the slopes of the Afanasyevskaya Mountains from the 2nd millennium BCE. Sites have revealed tombs marked with stone circles symbolizing the Sun God, later ones took the form of barrows or large mounds. Pottery in earlier graves consisted of elongated, spherical vessels with herringbone patterns, while later pottery was flat-bottomed.

context_nodes.label: Altai
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Altai as: Style and culture of the mountain range running along border shared by China and Mongolia.

context_nodes.label: Andronovo
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Andronovo as: Refers to the Neolithic culture established in the steppes of the Minusinsk basin during the 2nd and 1st millennia BCE. Sites have revealed earth houses designed for permanent habitation, with hearths for heating purposes and cooking. Bronze objects were also numerous, and workshops existed for working copper.

context_nodes.label: Karasuk
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Karasuk as: Refers to the Iron Age culture established in the Minusinsk basin on the Yenisey River from about 1200 BCE to about 70 BCE. Sites have revealed elbow-shaped knifes related to those used between the 14th and 11th centuries BCE in China during the Shang Period. Also notable are pillars with stylized ram heads or human figures.

context_nodes.label: Okunev
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Okunev as: Refers to the Eneolithic culture established in the steppes of the Minusinsk basin by Mongoloid peoples probably of Northern Siberian descent, from the beginning of the 2nd millennium BCE. Tombs have revealed a variety of stone sculptures.

context_nodes.label: Siberian Arctic Native styles
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Siberian Arctic Native styles as: Styles belonging to Siberian Arctic Native cultures.

context_nodes.label: Tashtyk
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Tashtyk as: Refers to the Eneolithic culture established in the Minusinsk Basin between the 1st century BCE and the 5th century CE. Notable artifacts from the period include examples of the Scynthian-Siberian Animal style on bronze and gold, and clay funeral masks portraying faces with a two-color decoration.

context_nodes.label: Tungus
context_nodes.summary: The Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus defines Tungus as: Culture and style of the indigenous Tungusic people native to the vast subarctic boreal forests (taiga) of Siberia and the Russian Far East, as well as parts of northern China and Mongolia.

context_nodes.label: Topological space
context_nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 22-00, 55-00, 54-00) states: A topological space is a set X together with a set 𝒯 whose elements are subsets of X , such that • ∅ ∈ 𝒯 • X ∈ 𝒯 • If U j ∈ 𝒯 for all j ∈ J , then ⋃ j ∈ J U j ∈ 𝒯 • If U ∈ 𝒯 and V ∈ 𝒯 , then U ∩ V ∈ 𝒯 Elements of 𝒯 are called open sets of X .

context_nodes.label: Manifold
context_nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 53-00, 57R50, 58A05, 58A07) states: Summary. A manifold is a space that is locally like ℝ n , however lacking a preferred system of coordinates.

context_nodes.label: Differential equation
context_nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 35-00, 34-00) states: A differential equation is an equation involving an unknown function of one or more variables, its derivatives and the variables.

context_nodes.label: Linear algebra
context_nodes.summary: PlanetMath (topic entry, MSC 15-00, 15-01) states: Linear algebra is the branch of mathematics devoted to the theory of linear structure .

context_nodes.label: Lemma
context_nodes.summary: PlanetMath (definition entry, MSC 00A05) states: There is no technical distinction a lemma, a proposition , and a theorem .
